teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: You are about to operate in a sandbox, but your workstation has more than one approved AWS context. Before issuing a resource-changing command, make the chosen context explicit. A profile name is a starting point for checking the caller, not a substitute for checking it.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A named AWS CLI profile groups credential and configuration settings; select it with --profile NAME.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Run aws sts get-caller-identity --profile NAME to inspect the caller ARN and account ID.

Run aws configure list --profile NAME to inspect the effective configuration and where its values came from; --region REGION overrides the configured Region for a command.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the exercise supplies a profile named lab-operator and expects a particular account. Run aws sts get-caller-identity --profile lab-operator. Suppose the illustrative result shows Account: [REDACTED_ACCOUNT] and Arn: arn:aws:iam::[REDACTED_ACCOUNT]:user/[REDACTED_OPERATOR]. Compare both values with the supplied operator context: this checks the caller identity and account. Then run aws configure list --profile lab-operator. Suppose its illustrative Region row shows Value: us-west-2, Type: config-file, Location: ~/.aws/config. This checks the effective Region and its configuration origin rather than inferring them from the profile's label. If the approved command targets a different Region, substitute that Region for REGION in its --region option. Keep the same explicit profile on the command. This example checks identity and effective configuration separately: knowing which account is selected does not answer which Region the command will use.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Do not treat an account check as a Region check. get-caller-identity inspects the caller ARN and account ID; configure list inspects effective configuration and its origins. --region overrides the configured Region for that command, not the meaning of the caller ARN.

video_need.reason: Comparing caller identity, effective configuration origins and an explicit Region override benefits from a short terminal demonstration.

teaching_notes: Keep credential creation out of scope; use supplied approved operator credentials and require the external secrets-handling preparation.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A lab needs two subnets for workloads placed in different Availability Zones. Address allocation has two separate questions: do the ranges fit without overlap, and does each range leave enough usable addresses? Complete the external IP-addressing and CIDR preparation before this AWS-specific allocation.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An IPv4 subnet CIDR must be within its VPC CIDR and must not overlap another subnet in that VPC.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
IPv4 subnet sizes range from /16 to /28; AWS reserves the first four addresses and the last address of each subnet.

Choose subnet ranges inside the VPC that do not intersect, and allow for the five reserved addresses when checking usable capacity.

Each subnet resides entirely in one Availability Zone; create separate subnets for workloads in different Availability Zones.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Take a supplied VPC range of 10.20.0.0/16. Two candidate subnets are 10.20.1.0/24 and 10.20.2.0/24. They lie inside that VPC and do not intersect. A /24 contains 256 addresses; after the five AWS reservations, 251 remain usable. For 10.20.1.0/24, the reserved addresses are .0 through .3 and .255. Compare 251 with the supplied capacity requirement, not 256. Place the two separate subnets in the two intended Availability Zones. Now consider changing the second candidate to 10.20.1.128/25: that range lies inside the first subnet, so it fails the nonoverlap check even though it is inside the VPC. Containment and nonoverlap are distinct tests, and both must pass.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A larger VPC does not make overlapping subnet ranges valid. Nor does an address count before reservations establish usable capacity. Check the VPC boundary, intersections with other subnets, and usable addresses separately; a subnet also belongs wholly to one Availability Zone.

video_need.reason: Nested and overlapping CIDR ranges plus reserved subnet addresses are easier to compare in an address-range diagram.

teaching_notes: Do not reteach CIDR arithmetic; require demonstrated external networking.ip_addressing_and_cidr mastery.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A team choosing a container platform asks who will operate each part of it. The useful comparison is not simply whether a service is managed. Identify which platform work the service handles and which workload work remains with the team.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: ECS is a managed container orchestration service that schedules container workloads; customers supply and operate their applications.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Managed EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane; customers retain responsibility for workload configuration and, depending on the compute option, worker nodes.

Choose between ECS and EKS by comparing the need for Kubernetes APIs and ecosystem with the team’s willingness to operate Kubernetes workloads.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Imagine an approved workload requirement that calls for Kubernetes APIs and its ecosystem. Managed EKS supplies the Kubernetes control plane, but the team still configures and operates Kubernetes workloads; worker-node responsibility depends on the selected compute option. Compare that requirement with an alternative that only needs managed container scheduling and can be operated through ECS. Record both the platform requirement and the remaining customer duties. The choice should reflect the team's willingness to operate those workloads, not just a preference for the word managed. This is an ownership comparison, not an exercise in administering a self-managed Kubernetes control plane.

For a second requirement, suppose the supplied application has no Kubernetes API dependency. That removes the stated platform reason for selecting EKS, but it does not remove the need to operate the application on ECS. Describe the remaining workload duty under both proposals. A comparison that says AWS manages everything for either service would hide the very ownership boundary the decision is meant to evaluate.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Managed does not mean the application is operated for you. ECS customers supply and operate applications; EKS customers retain workload configuration responsibilities and may retain worker-node duties. Keep that compute-option qualification when describing EKS ownership.

video_need.reason: The service comparison is an ownership classification; a compact responsibility table is enough and no tool demonstration is needed.

teaching_notes: Keep this comparison short; do not introduce self-managed Kubernetes administration.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A subnet's intended internet route has been added to a route table, yet the operator still needs to establish which table the subnet actually uses. Routing starts with association, then destination matching. Use the CIDR knowledge completed in external preparation.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A subnet uses its explicitly associated route table or, without an explicit association, the VPC main route table.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Among matching destination routes, the most specific destination prefix takes priority.

Associate the subnet with the intended route table and add an IPv4 0.0.0.0/0 route targeting the attached internet gateway for internet-bound destinations not matched by a more specific route.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the intended table contains a route for 10.20.0.0/16 and an internet-gateway route for 0.0.0.0/0. A destination of 10.20.2.10 matches both prefixes; the /16 is more specific, so the default route does not take priority. An example destination of 198.51.100.8 matches the default route when no more specific destination route applies. Before reasoning from those entries, inspect the subnet's association. If it has no explicit association, it uses the VPC main table, which may not be the table you edited. Associate the subnet with the intended table and check the default route's target is the attached internet gateway. The routing claim here is about the selected route, not a claim that every other requirement for a working connection has been met.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Adding 0.0.0.0/0 is not an instruction to override every other route. More specific matching destinations take priority. Also, editing a table is not proof that a subnet uses it: an explicit association or the main-table fallback determines that.

video_need.reason: A subnet association diagram and competing destination prefixes clarify main-table fallback and longest-prefix route selection.

teaching_notes: Teach route selection only; leave security rules and end-to-end connectivity diagnosis to their later concepts.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A business owner says a service may be unavailable briefly, but only a small amount of recent data may be lost. Those are two requirements, not one general promise of fast recovery. Name the tolerated downtime and tolerated data loss separately.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable time to restore service after a disruption.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.

Set recovery objectives from business requirements and use them to choose recovery capabilities that meet the tolerated downtime and data loss.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative requirement, suppose the owner accepts at most 30 minutes to restore service and at most 5 minutes of lost data. Record RTO as 30 minutes and RPO as 5 minutes. The first number answers how long service restoration may take after disruption; the second answers how much data loss, measured in time, is acceptable. A proposed recovery capability must be compared with both requirements. If its restoration time meets 30 minutes but its recoverable data is 20 minutes behind the disruption, it does not satisfy the stated data-loss objective. Conversely, sufficiently recent data does not by itself establish timely restoration. These numbers are example business requirements, not recommended AWS defaults.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: RPO is not another name for recovery duration. RTO bounds the time to restore service; RPO bounds acceptable data loss measured in time. Derive both from the business requirement rather than choosing whichever number is easiest to meet.

video_need.reason: RTO and RPO are two business-requirement definitions; a small timestamp comparison suffices without a tool demonstration.

teaching_notes: Keep measurement and rehearsal procedures for the later recovery-verification concept.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Two reports arrive in the operations queue: an EC2 operating-system update report and an RDS parameter-check report. To route the work correctly, look at what the service manages and what the customer still controls, rather than treating all managed services alike.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: With EC2, customers manage the guest operating system, including updates and security patches.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
With RDS, AWS manages database infrastructure and operating-system maintenance, while customers manage their data and application use.

Assign duties by the service boundary: AWS manages its infrastructure, while customers retain responsibilities for data, access and customer-controlled configuration.

Interpret the supplied EC2 OS-update report as customer guest-OS work and the supplied RDS parameter-check report as customer-controlled database configuration; RDS parameter groups contain database engine configuration values.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Label the EC2 report as customer guest-operating-system work, including updates and security patches. For the RDS report, distinguish AWS-managed database infrastructure and operating-system maintenance from the customer's data, application use and customer-controlled engine configuration. A parameter group contains database engine configuration values, so the supplied parameter-check report concerns customer-controlled configuration. In the handoff, name the service boundary alongside the report: guest OS for EC2, engine configuration values for this RDS check. That makes the assignment specific enough to act on without claiming the customer operates RDS infrastructure. Data and access responsibilities also remain part of the customer side of the boundary.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: AWS-managed infrastructure is not a blanket transfer of every operational duty. In particular, EC2 guest-OS patching remains customer work, while RDS operating-system maintenance is AWS work. RDS customer configuration and data duties still remain.

video_need.reason: EC2 and RDS responsibility boundaries can be communicated in a compact table without demonstrating platform operations.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce database capacity selection or specialist database administration.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: One requirement asks for more throughput during busy periods. Another asks for service to continue after a component fails. Both involve resources, but they ask different questions. Separate the amount of capacity from the independence of the capacity that remains after a failure.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Redundant components and multiple locations can keep a workload available when a component fails.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Capacity must accommodate workload demand; adding or removing resources helps match capacity to changing demand.

For a component-failure constraint, evaluate independent redundant capacity rather than merely increasing the size of the same component.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose a lab's demand requirement says it must handle 200 requests per second, while its failure requirement says it must keep serving after one component is lost. Increasing the size of a single component may address demand, but evaluating the failure requirement calls for independent redundant capacity. Write two conclusions: whether total capacity accommodates the supplied demand, and whether remaining independent components can meet the supplied service requirement after the loss. Adding or removing resources helps match changing demand; redundant components and multiple locations can support availability during a component failure. Keep the two requirements visible when comparing proposals, rather than accepting a larger component as the answer to both.

Now compare two illustrative proposals with equal total capacity: one larger component and two independent components. Under ordinary load they may both satisfy the supplied demand requirement. Under loss of the single larger component, its capacity is unavailable; with independent components, remaining capacity can be evaluated against the service requirement. Equal total capacity therefore does not settle the failure requirement. The record needs the surviving capacity question as well.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: More capacity in the same component is not the same as independent redundant capacity. For a component-failure constraint, evaluate the latter; for changing demand, evaluate whether the workload has enough capacity. One measure does not replace the other.

video_need.reason: A simple demand-versus-component-loss sketch suffices to distinguish capacity from independent redundant availability capacity.

teaching_notes: Defer specific scaling-policy and controlled-AZ-failure procedures.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An operator has an unresolved event and needs to know who can take responsibility. A resource name alone is not enough for a handoff. The response process needs an accountable owner and a defined next responder when routine work cannot resolve the issue.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Operational events need response processes with identified owners and escalation paths.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Assign event-response responsibility and document when and to whom unresolved issues are escalated.

Identify a team responsible for each resource and process so operators know whom to engage.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
For a sandbox orders service, suppose the supplied ownership record names the application operations team for the service and a separate team for an associated process. Use those named responsibilities when preparing the event-response record. Document the condition that requires escalation and identify the recipient rather than writing only escalate if necessary. If the current operator reaches the stated unresolved-issue condition, the record should show whom to engage and why. This example does not invent a universal escalation time or chain; the responsible teams and conditions come from the established environment. The operational value is that a later responder can find responsibility for both the resource and the process without guessing.

Compare an entry that says operations handles issues with one that names the responsible team, the unresolved-issue condition and the next responder. Only the latter gives the current operator a definite handoff decision under that condition. If responsibility for a process differs from responsibility for its resources, record both rather than assuming a single resource owner covers every operational activity.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: An escalation path is more than a list of contacts. The response process must document when an unresolved issue moves on and to whom. Naming a team for each resource and process supplies the ownership context for that decision.

video_need.reason: Ownership and escalation are documentation requirements; a small owner/condition/recipient table suffices without a tool demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use established owners and escalation conditions; do not author an organization-wide incident policy.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An operator requests a particular AWS action on a particular resource. A policy that looks permissive in general may not allow that request. Evaluate the request against the statement's actual action, resource and any conditions, using the access-control preparation already completed.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An identity-based policy attaches to an identity and specifies permitted or denied actions on resources.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
A statement uses Effect, Action and Resource, with optional Condition tests to scope when it applies.

For a request, compare action, resource and condition values with applicable statements; explicit deny overrides an allow, and absent an applicable allow the request is implicitly denied.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Consider supplied statements for an example object read. One Allow covers the requested action and the object's resource scope only when its Condition tests are satisfied. First compare the requested action with Action, then the target with Resource, then the request values with each applicable condition. If these checks do not find an applicable allow, the result is implicit deny. Now suppose an applicable Deny also covers the request: that explicit deny overrides the allow. Record which statement applies and which request values support the result rather than saying the policy allows reads in general. This example evaluates the identity-policy rules in this brief; it is not yet a full diagnosis of every policy type that can constrain AWS access.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: An Allow somewhere in a policy is not an allow for every request. Scope and conditions must match. An applicable explicit deny still wins over an allow, and no applicable allow leaves the request implicitly denied.

video_need.reason: A request-to-statement decision path makes scope, unsatisfied conditions, implicit deny and overriding explicit deny visible.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce session policies, boundaries or organization policies before their allowed contexts.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied delivery workflow needs a runner and an observable execution. Read the workflow as a description of when work begins, where each job runs and what each step does. Then use execution evidence to determine what actually happened.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Workflow YAML files are stored in .github/workflows; on defines the triggering events.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
jobs defines jobs, runs-on selects the runner, and steps lists actions invoked with uses or commands executed with run.

Inspect a workflow run’s job and step logs to verify which steps ran and which succeeded or failed.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: In an illustrative repository, locate the supplied YAML under .github/workflows. Read on to identify its triggering event, then locate the intended job under jobs. Its runs-on value selects that job's runner. In steps, distinguish an action referenced with uses from a supplied command executed with run. After the expected event, open that workflow run and inspect the job and step logs. Suppose the logs show two steps succeeded and the third failed: record those actual outcomes, not just the three steps declared in YAML. Keep the same run in view while following the evidence so that a log from another revision is not mistaken for this execution. The exercise uses supplied actions and commands, not independent application build logic.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Declared steps and completed steps are different evidence. The YAML describes the job and runner; the workflow run's logs establish which steps ran and whether they succeeded or failed. A runner selection alone is not proof of successful execution.

video_need.reason: Following one YAML job into runner selection and actual step logs benefits strongly from a workflow execution demonstration.

teaching_notes: Require external Git and pipeline-stage preparation; use supplied commands instead of introducing new shell syntax.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A delivery report shows deployments are more frequent, but recovery evidence is also changing. Read throughput and instability together before proposing a conclusion about the delivery workflow.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Deployment frequency measures how often changes are deployed; change lead time measures the elapsed time for a committed change to reach production.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Change fail rate measures the proportion of deployments requiring intervention; failed deployment recovery time measures how long recovery from a failed deployment takes.

Compare throughput and instability measures together over time and within application context rather than using one measure to rank individuals.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose one period has more deployments and shorter commit-to-production time, but a larger proportion of deployments need intervention. The first observations concern deployment frequency and change lead time; the latter concerns change fail rate. Add the failed-deployment recovery-time evidence to understand how long those failures take to recover from. Compare these measures over time for the same application context. Do not turn one improving measure into a ranking of individual operators.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Frequent delivery alone does not describe stability. Keep failure proportion and failed-deployment recovery time beside throughput measures, and interpret the combined evidence within the application's context.

video_need.reason: The bounded metric interpretation needs only a throughput/stability comparison over time, not a workflow execution demonstration.

teaching_notes: Keep metric definitions and interpretation bounded; do not introduce unsupported performance benchmarks.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An event rule should select the intended operational events without selecting unrelated examples. Build the matching requirement from named event fields, then test the boundary with examples that should pass and examples that should not.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An EventBridge event pattern describes event fields and values that an event must match.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Write a JSON object containing the fields to filter and arrays of acceptable values; fields omitted from the pattern are not required to match.

Test a pattern against both matching and nonmatching sample events with the EventBridge sandbox or TestEventPattern before using it in a rule.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the lab supplies events with source and detail-type fields. The intended pattern accepts source value lab.orders and detail-type value OrderReady. Represent each acceptable value in an array under its field in the JSON pattern. Test an event carrying those values, then change detail-type to OrderCancelled in a second sample and test again. Also test a sample that varies a field omitted from the pattern: omitted fields are not required to match. Compare each test result with the intended requirement before using the pattern in a rule. The names here are invented sample data; the event bus and real operational event fields must come from the supplied exercise. This stage teaches selection, not target execution permissions.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A pattern is not a requirement that every field in the event be identical to a sample. Fields omitted from the pattern are not required to match. Positive and negative tests make the intended field-level selection explicit.

video_need.reason: Side-by-side pattern JSON and positive/negative events make field matching and omitted-field behavior visible.

teaching_notes: Keep target authorization and delivery retries for their later concepts.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: The launch request for an EC2 lab instance is ready, but an operator must connect the approved choices with the resource that was actually created. Treat launch inputs, instance identity, lifecycle state and health evidence as distinct parts of the check.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Launching an EC2 instance requires choices such as AMI, instance type and network placement; an AMI supplies the initial software image.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
In the launch workflow, use the approved AMI, subnet and supplied IAM instance profile, then inspect the created instance’s ID and settings.

An instance profile contains an IAM role and attaches it to EC2; applications on the instance can use that role’s temporary credentials.

Inspect instance state and status checks to distinguish lifecycle state from reported host or instance health.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Use the exercise's approved AMI, instance type, subnet and supplied IAM instance profile in the launch workflow. The AMI supplies the initial software image; the instance profile attaches its role so applications can use temporary role credentials. After launch, record the created instance ID and compare its settings with the supplied choices. Next inspect instance state and status checks. If the state is running but a status check reports a problem, retain both observations: lifecycle state and reported host or instance health answer different questions. Do not replace the health evidence with the fact that a launch request completed. This is operation of the approved instance, not guest-OS configuration or independent role-policy design.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: An instance being in a running lifecycle state does not make status-check evidence redundant. Read state and status checks separately. Similarly, the instance profile attaches the role; it is not a separate set of embedded application access keys.

video_need.reason: Connecting launch inputs with instance identity, lifecycle state and status checks benefits from before-and-after console inspection.

teaching_notes: Require external compute preparation; defer detailed health diagnosis and Linux service configuration.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied deployment file must be stored and retrieved from the intended S3 location. Name both the bucket and the object key before transferring it, and keep the operator profile and Region explicit in the operation.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An S3 object consists of data and metadata and is identified within a bucket by its object key.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use aws s3 cp LOCAL_FILE s3://BUCKET/KEY --profile NAME --region REGION to upload, and reverse the source and destination to download.

A bucket is created in an AWS Region; verify the intended bucket location and caller access when storing or retrieving an object.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
For an illustrative transfer, let LOCAL_FILE be orders-release.zip and let KEY be releases/orders-release.zip in the approved bucket. Substitute the supplied bucket, profile and Region into the upload command. To download the same object, reverse the source and destination: the S3 reference becomes the source and the local file path becomes the destination. The object key identifies the object within its bucket; do not compare only the local filename when confirming which object was retrieved. Check the intended bucket location and caller access as part of the exercise. The command template teaches the two transfer directions without introducing an independent bucket-policy or object-recovery workflow.

Trace the upload and download endpoints before executing: upload has the local file as source and s3://BUCKET/KEY as destination; download reverses them. If the exercise expects releases/orders-release.zip, retrieving a different key is not a successful verification even when a file arrives locally. The intended location and transfer direction are checks you can make from the command arguments before inspecting its outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: The object key is scoped within a bucket. A familiar key string alone does not identify the intended storage location. Check the bucket's Region and the caller's access rather than assuming either from the file's name.

video_need.reason: A short transfer demonstration helps connect local paths with bucket/key paths, but the two direction templates are sufficient in text.

teaching_notes: Require external object-storage preparation; leave versioning and retention to later concepts.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An orders workload reports a metric, but the operator must select the same series that was published. The metric name is only part of that identity. Namespace and the full dimension combination also matter.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A custom CloudWatch metric is identified by its namespace, name and dimension combination.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Publish a metric with put-metric-data, specifying namespace, metric name, value and the intended dimensions.

Each distinct dimension combination identifies a distinct metric; query the same combination that was published to select the intended series.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the supplied metric is QueueDepth in namespace Lab/Orders with dimensions Environment=sandbox and Service=orders. Publish the supplied value with put-metric-data using that namespace, name and dimension combination. When querying, select that same combination. A second publication with Environment=staging and Service=orders identifies a distinct metric, even though its name is also QueueDepth. In the exercise record, write the namespace, name and dimensions beside the observed value. That makes the comparison about a particular series rather than a name shared by several series. These dimension values are illustrative workload labels; do not add new dimension combinations just to make the example more elaborate.

Consider a query using Environment=sandbox but omitting the supplied Service=orders dimension. It is not the same dimension combination as the example publication, so it does not identify that series by the stated identity rule. Compare complete combinations in the evidence record. This prevents a result from the staging series or another published combination from being described as the sandbox orders value.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Querying by a familiar metric name is not enough to establish that you selected the intended series. Each distinct dimension combination identifies a distinct metric. Compare the published and queried combinations, not just the displayed metric name.

video_need.reason: Publishing and locating distinct dimension combinations makes metric-series identity clearer than a metric-name-only screenshot.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce dimension-cost claims or alarm thresholds not present in the brief.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied fleet program receives target IDs from configuration. Before it may change resources, its validator needs an approved scope and a target limit. This task configures and exercises that validator; it does not ask you to write a new validation algorithm.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Process environment variables provide named string values that a supplied program can read as configuration.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Set the supplied allowlist environment variable FLEET_ALLOWED_INSTANCE_IDS to the approved comma-separated IDs and the supplied FLEET_MAX_TARGETS variable to the approved positive integer limit; these are configuration inputs to the supplied validator, not Python language keywords.

Exercise malformed and out-of-scope inputs and check the supplied validator rejects them before invoking a resource-changing operation.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the exercise approves two instance IDs and a maximum of two targets. Set FLEET_ALLOWED_INSTANCE_IDS to those IDs separated by commas and FLEET_MAX_TARGETS to the positive integer limit supplied for the task. Environment-variable values are strings the program reads as configuration. Run the supplied malformed-input case and a case containing an ID outside the approved list. Inspect the validator result and the supplied operation evidence to confirm rejection happened before a resource-changing call. Keep the approved IDs and limit visible alongside the test results. A label that sounds safe is not the check; the evidence is that the provided validator rejects malformed and out-of-scope input at the required boundary.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: FLEET_ALLOWED_INSTANCE_IDS and FLEET_MAX_TARGETS are configuration names understood by the supplied validator, not Python language keywords. Setting them is not proof of enforcement: exercise the rejection cases before enabling resource changes.

video_need.reason: A short supplied-validator demonstration helps show string configuration and rejection before mutation; the bounded rules are explicit in text.

teaching_notes: Use the supplied validator; do not author general-purpose Bash control flow or new Python parsing logic.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An approved CloudFormation template is ready to provision a new sandbox stack. Before execution, the operator needs a preview of the proposed resource actions and a clear separation between review and execution.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A change set previews proposed stack resource changes without executing them.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Review additions, modifications, removals and replacement indicators before authorizing execution; a preview does not guarantee that execution will succeed.

For a new stack, create a CREATE change set from the supplied template, wait for creation to complete, inspect it, and execute the approved set to provision the resources.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Create the supplied template's CREATE change set and wait until change-set creation completes. Inspect the proposed additions against the approved scope. For an illustrative new-stack review, suppose the preview contains the expected EC2 addition but also an extra addition the task does not authorize. Record that discrepancy for the approval decision rather than treating the preview as automatic authorization. When the set is approved, execute that specific set to provision the resources. A preview describes proposed changes without performing them, so retain execution evidence separately from the review. Even a preview that matches the requested scope does not guarantee execution will succeed.

A reviewer should be able to distinguish three records: the template and scope requested, the change-set actions previewed, and the later execution outcome. If the preview does not match the requested scope, execution should not be described as the approved change. If the preview matches but execution fails, preserve the failed outcome; the successful preview is not contradictory evidence because it was never a guarantee of execution success.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Creating a change set does not provision its resources. It previews changes without executing them. Likewise, a clean review is not a guarantee of execution success; inspect the preview before authorization and distinguish it from the later execution outcome.

video_need.reason: The preview-to-execution transition and resource replacement indicators benefit from a concrete change-set review demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use the supplied template and approval path; leave rollback diagnosis to its dedicated concept.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied policy should deny covered requests that are not MFA authenticated. The key question is what the condition means for the request's temporary credentials, including requests where the condition key is absent.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent condition indicates whether qualifying temporary credentials were authenticated with MFA.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
A Deny with BoolIfExists on aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent set to false can block non-MFA requests, including requests where the key is absent, subject to the statement’s scoped actions.

Apply the supplied scoped MFA policy and compare an allowed MFA-authenticated request with a denied request without MFA.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect the supplied Deny statement's scoped actions and its BoolIfExists test on aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent set to false. Compare two approved test cases: one using qualifying MFA-authenticated temporary credentials and one without MFA. The condition can block the latter, including a request where the key is absent, but only subject to the statement's action scope. Record the request context and result for each test. Do not describe the policy as covering every AWS action if its supplied scope covers only selected actions. The exercise is a comparison of allowed MFA-authenticated and denied non-MFA requests under the supplied policy, not a general redesign of human authentication.

Compare the action scope as well as the authentication context in the two test cases. A denial of one covered action without MFA supports the supplied scoped enforcement result; it does not establish denial of an action outside that statement. Similarly, a key-absent request falls under the stated BoolIfExists behavior, so absence must not be mistaken for a third automatically exempt authentication category.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: An absent key is not automatically outside a BoolIfExists Deny set to false. Keep that behavior and the statement's scoped actions together when explaining the result. Avoid turning this condition into an unqualified claim about all credentials or all requests.

video_need.reason: Contrasting MFA, non-MFA and absent-key requests against a scoped Deny condition clarifies the important condition boundary.

teaching_notes: Keep the qualifying-temporary-credential limitation; apply only the supplied scoped MFA policy.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A caller needs to enter a role, and that role needs permissions for the resulting session's work. These are different questions. Read trust as the role-entry boundary before evaluating what the assumed session may do.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A role trust policy identifies principals allowed to assume the role and any conditions for assumption.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Set Principal to the approved principal and Action to sts:AssumeRole with the supplied conditions in the role’s trust policy.

For cross-account assumption, the caller also needs permission to call sts:AssumeRole on the role; test approved and unapproved principals.

A role’s permissions policy controls what an assumed session may do, rather than who may assume it.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: For an approved cross-account caller, inspect the role trust policy's Principal, sts:AssumeRole action and supplied conditions. Then inspect the caller's permission to call sts:AssumeRole on that role. Test the approved principal and the supplied unapproved principal and retain their outcomes. Once a session is assumed, its allowed work is governed by the role's permissions policy rather than by treating the trust policy as an operations allowlist. For example, permitting entry to an orders-operator role does not itself describe which orders-resource actions that session may perform. The example keeps role entry and session permissions separate without inventing additional trust conditions or granting broader access.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A trust policy answers who may assume a role, not what an assumed session may do. Cross-account assumption also needs caller-side AssumeRole permission. An approved principal in the trust policy alone does not complete that cross-account permission check.

video_need.reason: A caller-to-role-to-session diagram separates trust entry, caller AssumeRole authority and session permissions.

teaching_notes: Use approved principals and supplied conditions; avoid advanced federation design.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A root-protection review is not a routine operating task performed with root. It checks that exceptional account authority is protected and that normal work uses non-root identities.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The AWS account root user has broad account authority and should not be used for routine tasks.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Protect root access with MFA and do not create root access keys; delete existing root access keys when they are no longer needed.

Review root-use and access-key evidence against the root-protection checklist, using non-root identities for routine operations.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Take the supplied root-use and access-key evidence and compare each item with the protection checklist. Confirm MFA protection in the review, note whether root access keys exist, and distinguish those keys from the non-root credentials used for routine operations. Do not create root access keys for the exercise. Existing root access keys that are no longer needed should be deleted under the approved process. Record findings against the checklist rather than using root to demonstrate ordinary resource operations. The purpose of the example is to interpret protection evidence and use the appropriate routine identity, not to explore every root-only capability.

The review should distinguish root access keys from root sign-in protection. An MFA finding answers the protection question, while the access-key evidence answers whether long-lived root keys exist and remain needed. A non-root identity used for the ordinary lab task supports the routine-use boundary. Keep these findings separate so one satisfactory item is not used to erase a problem in another item.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Broad account authority is not a reason to use root for convenience. Root should not be used for routine tasks. MFA protection and root-key hygiene belong in the protection review; ordinary operational testing belongs under non-root identities.

video_need.reason: Root protection is a short evidence checklist; no demonstration of privileged root operations is needed.

teaching_notes: Review supplied evidence; do not introduce or perform unapproved root-only operations.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A resource setting changed during a known interval, and the operator needs evidence of the actor and operation. Start with the selected Region and management-event history rather than assuming the record covers every kind of application activity.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: CloudTrail event history exposes recent management events for the selected Region; it does not represent all application activity.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Filter event history by an attribute such as event name, resource name or user name and the relevant time interval.

Inspect eventTime, eventName, userIdentity and requestParameters or resources to attribute a change to an actor, operation, target and time.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the supplied incident interval is 09:00 to 09:15 and identifies a resource name. Filter event history by the relevant attribute and time window, then inspect candidate events. For a matching change, read eventTime, eventName, userIdentity and requestParameters or resources. Record the actor, operation, target and time from those fields. If several nearby events exist, keep the target and operation comparison explicit rather than assigning the change to the closest timestamp alone. The example establishes attribution of an AWS management change; it does not establish the sequence of all application requests or supply application tracing.

For two candidate events in the interval, compare eventName and target evidence before assigning the change. One event may involve the same actor but a different target; another may involve the target but a different operation. Retain the event whose fields support the supplied change attribution. The record should make the actor, operation, target and event time inspectable together rather than reducing the result to a person's name.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: CloudTrail event history is not all application activity. It exposes recent management events for the selected Region. Keep that scope in the attribution record and derive the actor and target from event evidence, not from a guessed owner.

video_need.reason: A brief event-history walkthrough helps locate actor, target and time fields; the attribution procedure remains complete in text.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce X-Ray/request tracing or infer causation beyond the supplied change evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A cost report needs to distinguish orders-workload spend from other resource spend. A resource label can support that grouping only when the relevant cost-allocation tag has been activated for billing.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Cost-allocation tags categorize costs by resource-associated tag keys and values after activation for billing.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Activate the desired cost-allocation tag, then group Cost Explorer costs by that tag for the chosen period.

Resources without the relevant active tag can leave spend unallocated to the intended workload category.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the intended tag key is Workload and an approved value is orders. Activate that cost-allocation tag, then group Cost Explorer costs by it for the supplied period. Compare the orders category with spend not allocated to the intended category. If a resource lacks the relevant active tag, do not assign its spend to orders just because its name resembles the service name. Record the chosen period and tag grouping with the result. This is attribution of billed costs using resource-associated labels, not a new estimate of what the workload ought to cost. The example shows why activation and resource tagging both matter to the intended grouping.

Separate the labeling check from the billing-category check. The resource-associated Workload value states the intended category, while the active cost-allocation grouping shows how billed spend is categorized in the selected report. An unallocated category is evidence to investigate against missing relevant active tags, not permission to redistribute its amount by guessing. Keep the report's allocated and unallocated categories intact in the finding.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A label on a resource is not by itself the billing grouping check. Cost-allocation tags categorize costs after activation. Resources without the relevant active tag can leave spend unallocated, so the intended workload category may not contain all expected spend.

video_need.reason: Seeing active-tag categories beside unallocated spend helps interpretation, but the short activation/grouping explanation is sufficient.

teaching_notes: Defer workload cost estimation; use observed Cost Explorer evidence only.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An application writes structured events to a supplied file, and operators need those named fields in CloudWatch Logs. Follow one known event from its file source to the intended log stream rather than checking only that a log group exists.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A log group holds log streams with shared retention and access settings; a stream is a sequence of events from one source.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Configure the supplied log collector with the application file path, log group and stream name, and verify a known JSON event arrives in that stream.

CloudWatch Logs Insights can discover fields in JSON log events, so preserving structured event fields makes them queryable.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative orders event, the supplied JSON contains a request ID, an outcome and a timestamp. Configure the supplied collector with the application file path, intended group and intended stream name. Then verify that this known event appears in that stream with its structured fields preserved. The group provides shared retention and access settings, while the stream sequences events from a source. Named JSON fields can be discovered by Logs Insights, so preserving them supports later queries. Record the event identity and arrival location as the collection evidence. Do not claim that merely creating the group proves the collector sent the intended application event.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A log group and a log stream are not interchangeable labels. The group shares settings across streams; the stream holds a sequence of events from a source. Successful setup should include a known-event arrival check in the intended stream.

video_need.reason: Following one structured event from supplied file to the intended log stream demonstrates collection and preservation of named fields.

teaching_notes: Do not teach later query syntax here or redesign application logging.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A lab asks for one Linux service setting to change and supplies files for returning to the previous working configuration. Before activating anything, identify those rollback files and establish how the supplied checks will judge the change.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A configuration change needs validation of its intended effect and a defined way to return to the previous working configuration.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Identify and verify the supplied rollback files, change the supplied setting and run the supplied syntax or configuration check before activation.

Use the service’s supported reload or restart procedure to activate a valid change, then inspect status and the supplied effective-setting check; on failure restore and reactivate the saved configuration.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Imagine the approved change modifies a setting in the supplied service configuration. First identify and verify the supplied rollback files. Change only the supplied setting, then run the supplied syntax or configuration check before activation. For a valid change, use the service's supported reload or restart procedure. Inspect both service status and the supplied effective-setting check: the latter answers whether the intended setting took effect. If the change fails, restore and reactivate the saved configuration using the approved procedure. Keep the check results with the change record so that a restart request is not mistaken for a verified outcome. Linux filesystem, permission and service-operation preparation must already be complete; the supplied files do not replace that mastery.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Activation is not validation. A reload or restart request does not replace the syntax/configuration check before activation or the status and effective-setting checks afterwards. Returning to the saved configuration also requires reactivation, not just restoring a file.

video_need.reason: The configuration-check, activation, effective-setting verification and rollback transitions benefit from a controlled service demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied rollback files; do not teach backup creation, boot-startup policy or independent Bash authoring.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A release requirement allows only limited exposure to a new version and needs a way to return traffic to a known-good version. Compare delivery strategies by their replacement and traffic behavior, not by assuming one is always safest.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Rolling delivery replaces portions of the workload progressively rather than replacing all instances simultaneously.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Blue/green delivery maintains separate old and new environments and switches traffic to the new environment.

Canary delivery exposes a new version to a limited share of traffic before broader rollout.

Choose a strategy by comparing traffic exposure, available parallel capacity and the ability to return traffic to a known-good version.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Consider three proposals for the same approved release. Rolling replaces portions progressively. Blue/green maintains separate old and new environments and switches traffic. Canary exposes the new version to a limited traffic share before a broader rollout. Compare the supplied exposure constraint, available parallel capacity and rollback requirement with each proposal. If the requirement calls for separate old and new environments, the blue/green description directly addresses that arrangement. If it calls for limited initial traffic exposure, examine the canary proposal against that limit. Record how traffic can return to the known-good version under the supplied strategy instead of declaring that the strategy name guarantees recovery. The comparison is about stated requirements, not a universal ranking.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Rolling and canary are not simply two names for the same exposure pattern. Rolling describes progressive workload replacement; canary describes limited traffic exposure before broader rollout. Blue/green additionally uses separate old and new environments and a traffic switch.

video_need.reason: Traffic exposure and old/new capacity differ across strategies; animated replacement and traffic paths clarify the comparison.

teaching_notes: Defer product-specific rollout procedures; keep examples tied to stated exposure, capacity and rollback requirements.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A host signal should appear in CloudWatch under the correct instance identity. Use the supplied agent configuration to connect the chosen collection settings with a specific observed metric.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The CloudWatch agent collects configured host metrics and logs and sends them to CloudWatch.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
In the agent configuration, choose metrics under metrics_collected and append instance-identifying dimensions such as InstanceId.

Start the agent with amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl using fetch-config, the supplied configuration location and -s, then verify the expected metric and instance dimension in CloudWatch.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Choose the supplied host metrics under metrics_collected and append the intended InstanceId dimension. Start the agent through amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl with fetch-config, the supplied configuration location and -s. Then locate the expected metric in CloudWatch and compare its instance dimension with the approved host. A metric from a different instance is not verification for this host, even if the metric name matches.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Starting the agent is not the same as verifying collection. Check the expected metric and instance-identifying dimension in CloudWatch; the configuration describes what should be sent, while the observed series checks the intended host.

video_need.reason: A short agent setup and metric inspection helps connect configuration with InstanceId-specific output; text covers the bounded procedure.

teaching_notes: Use supplied configuration and agent-control procedure; require external package and Linux service preparation.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An alarm should reflect a supplied sequence of metric samples, including gaps. To explain its state, separate the statistic and threshold from the size of the evaluation window and the number of breaches required within it.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A metric alarm evaluates a statistic over periods against a threshold and has OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA states.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
EvaluationPeriods is the number of evaluated periods, and DatapointsToAlarm is the number of breaching datapoints required within that window.

Set the supplied metric, statistic, period, comparison operator and threshold along with the evaluation counts; compare the resulting state with the supplied samples.

Missing-data settings are breaching, notBreaching, ignore (retain current state), and missing (insufficient data when all datapoints are missing); missing is the default.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the approved samples for three evaluated periods are above, below and above the supplied threshold. Set EvaluationPeriods to 3 and DatapointsToAlarm to 2 for this example, alongside the supplied metric, statistic, period and comparison operator. There are two breaching datapoints in that window, matching the stated count requirement. Now examine the supplied missing-sample case with its selected missing-data policy. Do not silently treat a gap as a real zero or a real breach: use breaching, notBreaching, ignore or missing as configured. For the all-missing case, missing yields insufficient data; ignore retains the current state. Compare the resulting state with the supplied cases and retain the settings with the sample evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: EvaluationPeriods is not the number of breaches required. It is the number of evaluated periods; DatapointsToAlarm supplies the required breach count. Also, missing is the default missing-data setting, not a promise that every isolated gap immediately produces INSUFFICIENT_DATA.

video_need.reason: A sequence of sample windows, breach counts and missing-data states makes alarm evaluation behavior substantially clearer.

teaching_notes: Use supplied signals and thresholds; do not introduce unsupported sparse-data evaluation rules.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An operator needs approved human access without saving long-lived IAM user keys. Use the supplied Identity Center assignment and sign-in workflow, then test the access represented by the assignment.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: IAM Identity Center permission sets define permissions made available through assignments to users or groups in specified AWS accounts.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the supplied Identity Center assignment workflow to assign the approved user or group, account and permission set, then sign in to that account and test the intended access.

Configure a named SSO profile with aws configure sso and establish a session with aws sso login --profile NAME rather than storing long-lived IAM user keys.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: For a supplied operator group, select the approved AWS account and permission set in the assignment workflow. Sign in to that account and test the intended access. Configure a named SSO profile with aws configure sso, then establish its session with aws sso login --profile NAME using that profile's name. Keep the assigned account and permission set alongside the test result rather than treating a successful sign-in as the complete access check.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A permission set describes permissions made available through account assignments. The assignment and sign-in do not replace testing the intended access. Use the SSO session workflow rather than storing long-lived IAM user keys for this exercise.

video_need.reason: A short assignment/sign-in/profile walkthrough helps locate settings while the text fully specifies the approved-access checks.

teaching_notes: Use supplied assignments; do not create a new enterprise identity architecture.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A sandbox service should accept only its approved connection traffic. Build the required allow rule from the protocol, port range and source, then test the connection and its response. Apply the external ports/firewall preparation before this AWS rule exercise.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Security groups contain allow rules for traffic evaluated at associated network interfaces; they have no explicit deny rules.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Security groups are stateful: response traffic for an allowed connection is allowed regardless of rules in the response direction.

Add inbound rules specifying the required protocol, port range and approved source, remove unnecessary ingress, and test the required connections and their responses.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the supplied service requires TCP port 443 from an approved source range. Add that inbound allow rule on the associated security group and remove unnecessary ingress. Test the required connection and its response. For an allowed tracked connection, the response is allowed regardless of rules in the response direction because security groups are stateful. Keep the test about traffic the security group actually evaluates: Amazon-provided DNS and instance metadata traffic are not filtered by security groups. If the approved source is a security-group ID, it does not import that group's rules into the destination group. Use the supplied source and destination roles rather than widening ingress to make an unexplained test pass.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Security groups contain allow rules, not explicit deny rules. Also, a referenced source group does not contribute its own rule list to the destination group. Do not generalize the connection tests to traffic that security groups do not filter.

teaching_blocks.title: A boundary that changes the interpretation
teaching_blocks.content:
Security groups do not filter traffic to Amazon-provided DNS or EC2 instance metadata services.

Using a security-group ID as an allowed source does not import the referenced group’s rules into the destination group.

video_need.reason: A tracked request/response flow and source-group reference diagram clarify stateful behavior and filtering exceptions.

teaching_notes: Keep DNS/IMDS filtering exceptions explicit; do not imply security groups filter every AWS-service flow.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied EC2 instance specification must become a Terraform declaration with an approved provider version. Keep the provider selection, resource settings and execution review visible as separate parts of provisioning.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Declare resource "aws_instance" "NAME" with ami, instance_type and subnet_id set to the supplied values.

Run terraform init to install providers, terraform plan to inspect intended changes, and the approved terraform apply step to create the instance; verify the instance settings.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Replace APPROVED_VERSION in the provider declaration with the exact approved version. In the supplied aws_instance resource, use the supplied AMI, instance type and subnet ID; NAME is the declaration's chosen resource label. Run terraform init for provider installation, then terraform plan to inspect the intended instance changes. Compare those planned settings with the supplied specification before the approved apply step. After creation, inspect the live instance settings rather than accepting a syntactically plausible declaration as completion. This example teaches the bounded resource declaration and provider pin; it does not ask for an independent infrastructure design or a different provider version. The native EC2 foundation must be complete before interpreting these instance settings.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A provider pin and an instance declaration are not execution evidence. Initialization installs providers, planning inspects intended changes, and the approved apply creates the instance. Verification still needs the resulting instance settings.

video_need.reason: Provider pinning, declared EC2 settings and planned/live comparisons benefit from an annotated HCL-to-plan demonstration.

teaching_notes: Treat the HCL as a substitution template, not runnable with APPROVED_VERSION; do not introduce modules or backend configuration yet.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A caller's request reaches an S3 resource with a bucket policy. Evaluate the resource-side statement against that particular caller and target rather than treating an identity-policy allow as the whole resource-permission explanation.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A resource-based policy is attached to a resource and specifies the principals, actions and resources covered by its statements.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
For an S3 bucket policy, compare Principal, Action, Resource and Condition with the caller’s request; bucket and object ARNs identify different resource scopes.

Same-account identity and resource permissions can contribute allows, but applicable explicit denies override them; cross-account access generally requires permission on both sides.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Take a supplied object request and compare its caller with Principal, its operation with Action, its object ARN with Resource and its request values with Condition. A bucket ARN and an object ARN identify different scopes, so a statement about the bucket is not automatically a statement about that object request. For a same-account example, identity and resource permissions can contribute allows, but an applicable explicit deny overrides them. For the supplied cross-account example, keep the qualification that access generally requires permission on both sides. Record the matching scope and applicable deny evidence without turning that general cross-account rule into an exhaustive account of every special case.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A resource policy is attached to the resource and includes principal scope; it is not simply an identity policy moved to another file. Also, an applicable explicit deny still overrides contributed allows. Keep bucket and object ARN scopes distinct.

video_need.reason: Caller and bucket/object scope diagrams clarify resource-policy matching, cross-account qualifications and explicit-deny precedence.

teaching_notes: Preserve generally for cross-account requirements; avoid advanced grant exceptions not in this brief.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An account-onboarding request provides approved inputs and baseline checkpoints. Completing account creation is only part of the governed onboarding task; enrollment, placement and controls need evidence too.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Account Factory provisions and enrolls accounts into a governed landing zone using standardized account settings.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Execute the established provisioning workflow with the approved account inputs and inspect the account’s enrollment and organizational-unit placement.

Verify the supplied baseline checkpoints against the account’s applied controls; creating an account alone does not demonstrate governance completion.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Execute the established Account Factory workflow with the supplied account settings. Inspect the new account's enrollment and organizational-unit placement, then compare the applied controls with each supplied baseline checkpoint. If creation completed but a checkpoint has no supporting result, keep that distinction in the record. The account exists, but governance completion has not yet been demonstrated by the stated checks.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A created account is not automatically proof of completed governance. Verify enrollment, intended organizational-unit placement and supplied baseline checkpoints against the account's actual applied controls.

video_need.reason: A short established onboarding walkthrough helps locate enrollment, OU placement and control evidence; no architecture lesson is needed.

teaching_notes: Execute the established workflow only; do not design a landing zone or invent baseline controls.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied Python automation script has a requirements file. Before running it against AWS, prepare an isolated dependency environment and confirm the intended operator context.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A virtual environment isolates the Python interpreter context and installed packages used by an application.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Create one with python -m venv ENV_DIR and activate it using the platform’s activation command, such as source ENV_DIR/bin/activate on Unix.

Install supplied dependencies with python -m pip install -r requirements.txt inside the environment, inspect them with python -m pip list, and run the supplied script with that interpreter.

Confirm the approved AWS profile and Region through the supplied credential configuration before running AWS automation.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Use python -m venv ENV_DIR with the supplied directory name, then activate it with the command for your platform; source ENV_DIR/bin/activate is the Unix example. Inside that environment, install requirements.txt with the stated pip command and inspect the package list. Run the supplied script with that environment's interpreter only after confirming the approved AWS profile and Region through its credential configuration. Record the environment and context used alongside the script outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Dependency isolation and AWS target selection are separate checks. A virtual environment isolates interpreter context and installed packages; it does not replace confirming the approved AWS profile and Region.

video_need.reason: A short environment and dependency setup demonstration helps locate the active interpreter, but the supplied command sequence suffices in text.

teaching_notes: Require external Python and shell preparation; activation paths are platform-specific templates.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An inventory task needs all results in one approved account and Region. Page controls affect how results are retrieved or bounded, so read them before claiming that a listing is complete.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The AWS CLI automatically follows service-side pagination for supported commands unless automatic pagination is disabled.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use an explicit --profile and --region with --output json for structured inventory and avoid --no-paginate when the full listing is required.

--page-size changes service-call page size rather than the total output count; --max-items limits output and a returned NextToken must be resumed with --starting-token when manually collecting the remainder.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Run the supplied supported inventory command with explicit profile and Region and JSON output. For the full listing, keep automatic pagination enabled rather than adding --no-paginate. If the exercise deliberately uses --max-items to collect a bounded portion, retain the returned NextToken and resume with --starting-token for the remainder. Changing --page-size adjusts service-call page size; it is not the same as limiting total output with --max-items. Keep the continuation evidence with the inventory.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A smaller page size does not mean a smaller total inventory. Distinguish service-call page size from the output limit, and do not discard a continuation token when manually collecting the remainder.

video_need.reason: A brief page-size/output-limit comparison helps interpret continuation tokens; the bounded pagination rules are fully stated in text.

teaching_notes: Apply pagination only to supported commands; do not invent an inventory command or API continuation format.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
