teaching_blocks.content: Another operator must perform a known task without relying on your memory. A useful runbook makes the conditions for acting and the evidence for advancing explicit.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A runbook documents procedures for a known operational outcome and should be usable by the operator performing the task.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Write the task’s preconditions, ordered actions and expected results so execution can be checked rather than inferred.

Include failure-handling and escalation instructions identifying when routine execution must stop and who takes over.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: For a supplied restart task, write its preconditions, approved ordered actions and expected results from the established procedure. Include the condition that stops routine work and name the escalation recipient. Read the draft as the receiving operator: can each expected result be checked before advancing? Replace an instruction such as confirm it worked with the supplied observable result. Do not invent a recovery action outside the approved procedure.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A list of actions alone is not an actionable runbook. Preconditions, expected results and failure/escalation instructions are needed so the operator can check execution rather than infer success.

video_need.reason: The handoff is a short document structure and expected-result check; a sample runbook table suffices.

teaching_notes: Use established procedures and owners; defer live incident execution to the later runbook-recovery concept.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied EKS workload has a Pod that appears to be running. The operator still needs evidence about its containers and events. Pod phase is one lifecycle observation, not a complete health diagnosis.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A Pod groups containers with shared networking and storage and has a lifecycle distinct from the controller that may replace it.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Pod phases include Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed and Unknown; phase alone is not a complete diagnosis of container health.

Use kubectl get pod NAME, kubectl describe pod NAME and kubectl logs NAME -c CONTAINER to inspect status, scheduling or runtime events and container output.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Using the supplied cluster access setup, substitute the approved Pod name into kubectl get pod NAME. Record its phase, then inspect kubectl describe pod NAME for scheduling or runtime events. Use kubectl logs NAME -c CONTAINER for the intended container's output. Suppose the phase reads Running while the supplied events and logs show a container problem. Preserve those observations together rather than deciding that Running settles health. A Pod groups containers with shared networking and storage; its lifecycle is distinct from a controller that may replace it. This exercise inspects the Pod and its container output, not the controller's desired-replica reconciliation or cluster administration.

If the Pod is Pending, use its described scheduling events as evidence rather than applying a correction inferred from the phase label alone. If it is Running, inspect the intended container's runtime events and output. The same inspection sequence accommodates different phases because it records what happened at the Pod and container boundaries. An unrelated container's output is not evidence about the one named in the exercise.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Running is a Pod phase, not a complete diagnosis of container health. Other phases include Pending, Succeeded, Failed and Unknown, but the phase list does not replace inspection of events and the intended container's logs.

video_need.reason: Pod phase, runtime events and container logs are separate changing observations that benefit from a live inspection demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied cluster access; leave Deployment reconciliation and self-managed cluster administration out of scope.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A managed database is available for an approved connection test. Verify the intended instance and the data marker separately; a resource status does not answer whether the expected application data is present.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An RDS DB instance has an identifier, engine, endpoint and operational status that can be inspected in the console or through describe-db-instances.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect the intended DB instance and verify its engine and status before attempting the supplied database connection.

Connect using the supplied endpoint, database client and approved credentials, then run the supplied query to check the data marker; instance status alone does not verify application data.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Locate the supplied DB instance identifier in the console or describe-db-instances result. Compare its engine and operational status with the exercise requirements before using the supplied endpoint, client and approved credentials. Run the supplied query and retain its data-marker result. If the status is acceptable but the query does not return the expected marker, report that distinction rather than calling the data check successful. Record the instance identity and endpoint with the safe query outcome so the test can be tied to the intended database. This is bounded database operation with a supplied query, not a lesson in authoring SQL or selecting database capacity.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: An acceptable instance status does not verify application data. The instance inspection checks identity, engine and status; the supplied connection and query check the data marker. Neither result should be used as a substitute for the other.

video_need.reason: A brief instance-to-endpoint walkthrough helps tie the safe query to the intended database; text covers the supplied check.

teaching_notes: Use supplied client and query; do not teach SQL syntax or database capacity selection.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An S3 object was overwritten or simply deleted, and the lab requires an earlier version to remain recoverable. Versioning, restoration method and lifecycle expiry all affect the available recovery path.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: S3 versioning retains multiple versions of an object, including versions displaced by overwrites.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
In a versioning-enabled bucket, a simple delete ordinarily creates a delete marker rather than removing prior versions; deleting a specified version permanently removes it.

To restore an overwritten object, copy the selected prior version to the same key to create a new current version; to undo a simple deletion, remove its delete marker to expose the preceding version.

Inspect noncurrent-version expiration and other lifecycle rules so required recoverable versions remain for the required window.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the approved bucket contains two versions of releases/orders.zip and the newer one overwrote the earlier content. Select the required prior version and copy it to the same key; that creates a new current version with the selected content. For a separate simple-deletion case, inspect the delete marker and remove that marker to expose the preceding version. These are different recovery operations, so identify the actual case before acting. Inspect noncurrent-version expiration and other supplied lifecycle rules against the required recovery window. A retained prior version is useful only while it remains available under those controls. Do not delete a specified needed version: that operation permanently removes that version.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A simple delete in a versioning-enabled bucket ordinarily creates a delete marker; it is not equivalent to permanently deleting a specified version. Keep ordinarily in the explanation, and check lifecycle rules rather than assuming versioning alone preserves every version indefinitely.

video_need.reason: Version lists, delete markers and recovery actions benefit from a controlled before-and-after object restoration demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use approved versions and recovery window; distinguish marker removal from copying a prior version.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An already-built container image must reach an approved repository and then be retrieved as the exact published content. Keep the publication reference and the content digest separate in the evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: ECR stores container images in repositories and assigns image digests that identify image content.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Authenticate Docker with aws ecr get-login-password --region REGION piped to docker login --username AWS --password-stdin REGISTRY.

Tag the already-built image with REGISTRY/REPOSITORY:TAG and run docker push with that reference.

Use docker pull REGISTRY/REPOSITORY@sha256:DIGEST to retrieve the exact image and verify publisher and consumer access with their approved identities.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Substitute the supplied Region and registry in the authentication pipeline from get-login-password to docker login. Tag the already-built image with the approved REGISTRY/REPOSITORY:TAG and push that reference. Record the published image digest, then use the supplied digest in docker pull REGISTRY/REPOSITORY@sha256:DIGEST for the consumer test. Verify publisher and consumer access with their respective approved identities rather than using one identity for both roles. The digest identifies image content, while the repository and tag provide the publication reference in this exercise. The task begins with a built image and does not ask for Dockerfile authoring or a new container build process.

Write the publication and consumption references side by side: the push uses REGISTRY/REPOSITORY:TAG, and the exact-content pull uses REGISTRY/REPOSITORY@sha256:DIGEST. Verify that the digest is the one recorded after publishing. Testing publisher push permission does not establish consumer pull permission, so preserve both identity-specific outcomes. This separates content identity from the two access roles without rebuilding the supplied image.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Publication is not the same as verified consumption. Push with the approved publisher, then retrieve the exact digest under the approved consumer and check its access. Do not substitute a convenient tag for the stated exact-content retrieval test.

video_need.reason: Publishing a tagged image and retrieving its exact digest under different identities benefits from an end-to-end terminal demonstration.

teaching_notes: Require external Docker and shell-pipe preparation; commands are supplied-value templates.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A release needs more than a downloadable build file: the operator must connect the exact content with its source and build provenance. Follow one supplied output through attestation, immutable publication, download and provenance verification.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An artifact attestation binds provenance such as source repository, revision and build workflow to an artifact digest.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
For a supplied output file, set workflow permissions id-token: write, contents: read and attestations: write, generate provenance with actions/attest@v4 and subject-path set to the file, then publish it with actions/upload-artifact@v4 using path set to that file and name set to the supplied revision-based version; retain the workflow run, artifact name and upload’s SHA256 digest as the immutable content reference, since v4 artifacts are immutable.

Download the published artifact with actions/download-artifact, which checks the upload’s SHA256 digest and warns on mismatch, then verify the extracted output file’s provenance with gh attestation verify PATH/TO/YOUR/BUILD/ARTIFACT-BINARY -R ORGANIZATION_NAME/REPOSITORY_NAME --format json and inspect the verified attestation for the source revision and build workflow/run before deployment.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the supplied output is an orders release file for revision rev-42. Use that file as subject-path for actions/attest@v4 with the stated workflow permissions. Publish the same file through actions/upload-artifact@v4 using its path and the supplied revision-based name. Retain the workflow run, artifact name and upload SHA256 digest as the content reference. Download it through actions/download-artifact and inspect any digest-mismatch warning; that action checks the upload digest. Then run the stated gh attestation verify template on the extracted output file for the approved repository. Inspect the verified JSON attestation for source revision and build workflow/run before deployment. The example keeps download-integrity evidence and provenance evidence connected to the same output rather than treating either one alone as the entire traceability record.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A digest check and provenance verification answer different questions. Download checks the upload SHA256 digest and warns on mismatch; the verified attestation provides source and build context. Do not claim the download action itself blocks every mismatch or proves the intended source revision.

video_need.reason: Artifact upload, digest check and verified attestation provenance are linked evidence views that benefit from a single continuous demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use actions/attest@v4, not a substituted action; preserve the warning behavior and verify the extracted output file.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied CloudFormation S3 template needs one approved property change. Read the declaration and references first, then verify that the live resource reflects the approved template rather than stopping at template validation.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A CloudFormation template’s Resources section declares resources by logical ID, Type and Properties.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
An S3 bucket declaration uses Type: AWS::S3::Bucket; Ref on its logical ID returns its bucket name.

Modify the supplied declared property and references, validate with aws cloudformation validate-template --template-body file://TEMPLATE, and create the sandbox stack from the approved template.

Inspect stack events and outputs and the bucket’s live property to confirm the declaration was deployed.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Find the bucket's logical ID in Resources and inspect its Type and Properties. Type: AWS::S3::Bucket declares the bucket, and Ref on that logical ID returns its bucket name. Modify only the supplied property and references, then substitute the template file path in validate-template. Create the approved sandbox stack and inspect stack events and outputs. Finally, check the bucket's live value for the changed property. Keep declaration, deployment evidence and live-property evidence together: a correct-looking template is the requested state, while the live inspection checks what was deployed. This exercise uses the supplied standard template rather than introducing a new infrastructure language or unrelated resources.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Template validation is not verification of the bucket's live property. Inspect stack events, outputs and the deployed property after creating the sandbox stack. Also, Ref on an S3 bucket logical ID returns the bucket name, not an invented object reference.

video_need.reason: Template declaration, Ref output and live bucket-property verification benefit from an annotated template-to-stack demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use the supplied property; do not introduce new resource types or template functions.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A runtime consumer needs a managed secret, but the operator must verify use without revealing the value. Check the consumer's safe result rather than displaying the secret.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Secrets Manager stores protected secret values and returns them to authorized consumers at runtime.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Retrieve a secret through GetSecretValue using the supplied secret identifier and approved runtime identity, with secretsmanager:GetSecretValue permission.

Use the retrieved value in the runtime consumer without writing it into source code or logs; verify success through the consumer’s safe result rather than displaying the value.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Use GetSecretValue with the supplied secret identifier under the approved runtime identity with secretsmanager:GetSecretValue permission. Feed the returned value to the supplied consumer and inspect its safe success result. Keep the secret out of source code and logs. The example verifies authorized runtime retrieval and use; it does not require copying the value into a debugging transcript.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Displaying a secret is not necessary evidence of successful retrieval. Use the consumer's safe result to verify success and do not write the value into source code or logs.

video_need.reason: A short safe-consumer example helps distinguish retrieval from secret display; the text fully states the boundary.

teaching_notes: Do not teach managed-secret rotation; do not show example secret values.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A team has several complaints about delivery, but the exercise asks for one evidence-backed improvement. Select a bottleneck supported by the supplied record and define a measurable result before proposing the change.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Continuous improvement uses feedback and measured outcomes to identify and address delivery friction.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Identify a bottleneck supported by the supplied delivery evidence and propose one bounded change with a measurable expected outcome.

Compare the success signal before and after the change to determine whether the intervention improved the intended outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose supplied delivery records show that a particular review handoff is the measured bottleneck. Propose one bounded change to that handoff and state the success signal the evidence will compare. Record the baseline for that signal, apply the approved change, then compare the after-change signal with the baseline. If the chosen measure does not improve, do not call the intervention successful merely because the change was completed. Keep the conclusion about this bottleneck and measured outcome, not about every aspect of delivery. The example does not assume a particular improvement always works; feedback and measured results determine whether it helped.

If the after-change success signal worsens or remains unchanged, report that observed result instead of replacing the chosen measure with a more flattering one. The intervention was justified by one observed bottleneck and one expected outcome; the comparison should retain that same outcome. A completed action can be useful feedback even when it fails to produce the anticipated improvement.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Implementing a change is not proof of improvement. Identify the evidence-supported bottleneck, state the expected measurable outcome and compare its success signal before and after. A general preference for automation is not the missing measurement.

video_need.reason: One bottleneck and its before/after success signal can be compared in a small evidence table without a tool demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied delivery evidence; avoid inventing performance targets or attributing results to individuals.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A Config rule reports a noncompliant resource. Before choosing a response, establish which recorded configuration differs from the rule's desired conditions and what the governing policy permits.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: AWS Config rules evaluate recorded resource configuration against desired conditions and report compliance results.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Open the rule’s noncompliant resources and inspect the affected resource, evaluation result and rule parameters to identify the configuration mismatch.

Choose the established remediation or escalation path from the governing policy rather than treating a compliance result as proof of an attack.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Open the supplied rule's noncompliant-resource result and record the resource identity. Compare the evaluation result and rule parameters with the affected resource's recorded configuration. Suppose the mismatch is a supplied setting outside the rule's required value; describe that setting mismatch rather than labeling the resource attacked. Choose the established remediation or escalation path from the governing policy. Preserve the evaluation evidence with that choice so the next operator can see why the response was selected. This is basic configuration-finding triage, not proof of malicious activity or permission to apply an unapproved change.

For a supplied noncompliant result, distinguish the rule's required value from the resource's recorded value. If the rule parameters differ from what the operator expected, include that discrepancy in triage rather than silently comparing with a different criterion. The governing policy determines whether the next action is remediation or escalation. The compliance evidence establishes a configuration mismatch, not an attacker or a cause of compromise.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A compliance result reports configuration against desired conditions; it is not proof of an attack. Read the resource, evaluation and parameters before choosing the policy-governed remediation or escalation path.

video_need.reason: A brief rule-result and recorded-configuration comparison helps locate mismatch evidence; the response decision remains explicit in text.

teaching_notes: Do not infer compromise or design specialist security remediation.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A stack's bucket property was changed outside CloudFormation in the controlled lab. Drift detection can show a declared-versus-current difference, but the operator must understand what it checked and what it did not do.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: CloudFormation drift detection compares supported explicitly declared resource properties with their current values.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Run drift detection on the provisioned stack after the supplied out-of-band change, wait for completion and inspect the bucket’s expected and actual property values.

Drift detection reports differences without repairing them; unsupported or undeclared properties may not be checked.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Run drift detection on the provisioned stack after the supplied out-of-band change and wait for completion. Locate the bucket's result and compare its expected and actual property values. Write the difference as a pair, such as supplied declared value A and current value B, rather than saying only drifted. Detection compares supported explicitly declared properties; unsupported or undeclared properties may not be checked. Keep that scope beside the result so a lack of reported drift is not described as exhaustive verification of every property. This task observes and records the difference. It does not repair the resource merely by running detection.

A useful drift record names the stack resource, the specific checked property and its expected/actual pair. If another setting is not explicitly declared or supported for comparison, do not infer its correctness from this result. This lets the next operator see exactly what detection established. Running detection again without changing the resource does not perform the missing repair; detection and approved correction are different actions.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Drift detection reports differences without repairing them. It also does not promise to check every property: supported, explicitly declared properties are the comparison scope, and unsupported or undeclared properties may not be checked.

video_need.reason: Expected-versus-actual resource properties and drift-detection status benefit from a before-and-after inspection demonstration.

teaching_notes: Keep detection distinct from repair; do not extend drift coverage beyond supported declared properties.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A controlled stack update failed. The response needs both the original failure evidence and the rollback outcome; a final stack label alone can hide the sequence that explains the problem.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: CloudFormation stack events record resource operation status and failure reasons during an update.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
After the supplied controlled update failure, inspect the first failing resource event and subsequent rollback events.

UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE indicates rollback to the previous working stack state; UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED requires resolving the rollback failure before continuing.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect the supplied update's stack events, starting with the first failing resource event and its failure reason. Then follow subsequent rollback events. If the resulting status is UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, describe rollback to the previous working stack state. If it is UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED, the rollback failure must be resolved before continuing. Retain the first failure and the rollback status separately in the record so that the update problem is not confused with a later rollback problem. Use the supplied controlled failure and approved response path rather than experimenting with new changes while the rollback outcome is unresolved.

For an illustrative event sequence, suppose the update first reports a resource failure and later reports a rollback failure. The first event explains why the requested update did not complete; the later event explains why rollback did not complete. Preserve both reasons in their event order. Resolving only the first update problem does not justify ignoring the status that says rollback failure still needs resolution before continuing.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED is not another success label for rollback. It requires resolving the rollback failure before continuing. Conversely, UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE describes rollback to the prior working stack state, not successful deployment of the failed update.

video_need.reason: The first failure and subsequent rollback events form a changing sequence best clarified through one controlled stack update.

teaching_notes: Do not invent failure-recovery commands; inspect supplied events and established resolution guidance.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An EC2 application needs the approved role rather than embedded access keys. Attach the role through its instance profile, then test the resulting identity and bounded permissions from the instance.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An instance profile contains one IAM role and provides a way to pass that role to EC2.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use associate-iam-instance-profile to attach the approved instance profile to an EC2 instance without an existing association. To replace an existing profile, use the console’s Modify IAM role workflow instead.

Use the instance’s role credential provider rather than embedded keys, inspect the caller identity and test one allowed and one denied operation under the assigned role’s permissions.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: For attachment to an instance without an existing association, use the supplied associate-iam-instance-profile operation. For replacement of an existing profile, use the console’s Modify IAM role workflow to select the approved role. The profile contains one IAM role. From the instance, use the role credential provider, inspect caller identity and test one supplied allowed operation and one denied operation. Record the assigned role context with those outcomes. Merely seeing an attached profile is not the full permission test for the application.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: An instance profile is the container used to pass one role to EC2, not a reason to embed keys. Test application operations under the role credential provider and inspect caller identity rather than assuming the attachment proves the intended access.

video_need.reason: A short profile-attachment and caller/permission check helps locate the relevant identity evidence, while text specifies both tests.

teaching_notes: Use the approved role and supplied test operations; do not design unrelated policies.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied EKS workload needs AWS access under a particular role. Tie the association to the intended cluster, namespace and service account, then test both the associated and unassociated workload cases.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: EKS Pod Identity associates a Kubernetes service account in a namespace and cluster with an IAM role for application AWS access.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Create an association for the supplied cluster, namespace, service account and approved role; run the workload with that serviceAccountName.

The Pod Identity agent and supported SDK credential chain supply temporary role credentials to associated Pods; verify allowed access from the intended workload and rejection from an unassociated workload.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Create the approved Pod Identity association using the supplied cluster, namespace, service account and role. Run the workload with that serviceAccountName. The Pod Identity agent and supported SDK credential chain supply temporary role credentials to associated Pods. Verify the intended workload's allowed AWS access and the supplied unassociated workload's rejection. Keep the workload identity and association scope beside the results so access observed from one Pod is not assigned to another.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A role's existence is not the workload association. The association names a service account in a namespace and cluster, and the workload must use that serviceAccountName. Preserve the agent and supported-SDK qualifications when describing credential delivery.

video_need.reason: The cluster/namespace/service-account association and credential path benefit from a workload-identity diagram plus test evidence.

teaching_notes: Use supplied agent/access setup; do not introduce a different workload-identity mechanism.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A GitHub Actions workflow should enter an approved AWS role without stored AWS access keys. The trust boundary must identify the approved token context rather than accepting any workflow that can request a token.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: GitHub Actions OIDC enables a workflow to obtain temporary AWS role credentials without storing AWS access keys.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Configure the GitHub token issuer as an IAM OIDC provider and constrain the role trust policy’s aud and sub claims to the approved audience and repository/branch or environment.

Give the workflow id-token: write permission and configure the AWS credential action to assume the approved role; test that an unapproved repository or branch cannot assume it.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Configure the supplied GitHub token issuer as the IAM OIDC provider. In the role trust policy, compare aud and sub with the approved audience and repository/branch or environment. Give the workflow id-token: write permission and configure the supplied AWS credential action to assume that role. Then run the approved case and the supplied unapproved repository or branch case. Verify the latter cannot assume the role. This test makes the trust scope observable rather than treating temporary credentials alone as evidence that only the intended workflow can get them.

The negative test should differ in the repository, branch or environment context that the supplied sub condition restricts. A successful approved case plus a rejected unapproved case supports that exact trust boundary. Check the audience separately rather than treating a matching subject as evidence that every trust test passed. The AWS credential action's success must be read with the approved token context and role target.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Avoiding stored keys does not remove the trust-policy check. Constrain aud and sub to the approved context and test an unapproved repository or branch. A workflow's id-token permission alone does not establish the intended AWS role trust boundary.

video_need.reason: Audience/subject trust restrictions and approved/unapproved workflow tests benefit from annotated policy and workflow context.

teaching_notes: Keep this GitHub OIDC mechanism separate from CodePipeline service-role trust.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An operator assumes an approved role for a bounded session. The returned credentials have three fields and an expiry, and the permissions explanation must keep role-policy grants distinct from resource-based grants.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Temporary AWS credentials consist of an access key ID, secret access key and session token and expire after their issued lifetime.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Call aws sts assume-role with --role-arn, --role-session-name and the approved --duration-seconds, then use all three returned credential fields and inspect Expiration.

Permissions granted through a role’s identity-based policies are intersected with any session policies; resource-based grants are evaluated separately, and grants directly to the session ARN are not limited by session policies; an explicit deny in any applicable policy overrides an allow.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Substitute the approved role ARN, session name and duration in the assume-role command. Use the returned access key ID, secret access key and session token together, and inspect Expiration. If a session policy is supplied, role identity-policy permissions are intersected with it. Do not extend that sentence to every resource grant: resource-based grants are evaluated separately, and grants directly to the session ARN are not limited by session policies. An applicable explicit deny still overrides an allow. Record the issued lifetime and the supplied permission evidence without displaying credential values. This example teaches session composition and the stated grant distinctions, not a new policy intended to exercise every possible permission case.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Temporary credentials are not just an access-key pair: the session token is also required, and the issued lifetime ends. Likewise, session-policy intersection describes role identity-based grants; it is not an unqualified limit on all resource-based grants.

video_need.reason: Session lifetime and identity/session/resource-grant distinctions benefit from a credential timeline and policy-evaluation diagram.

teaching_notes: Do not expose credential values; preserve direct-session-ARN and explicit-deny qualifications.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An event pattern matches the right event, but that does not authorize the target operation. Determine the target's required permission model before assigning execution authority.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: EventBridge target execution authority is separate from the event pattern that selects events.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
For targets requiring an execution role, grant events.amazonaws.com permission to assume the role and attach permissions scoped to the approved target operation and resource.

Targets such as SNS and Lambda use resource-based permissions for invocation; use the target’s required authorization model rather than assuming every target uses a role.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
For a supplied target that requires an execution role, grant events.amazonaws.com the approved trust to assume it and scope role permissions to the approved operation and resource. For a supplied SNS or Lambda target, use the required resource-based invocation permissions instead. Compare the selected target with its authorization model in the record. The selection pattern determines which events match; the separate authority determines whether the intended target operation is permitted. Do not assign a role to every target just because a different target used one.

For a target requiring an execution role, inspect both trust and scoped operation/resource permission. Trust permits EventBridge to assume the role; the role's permissions cover the approved target action. For the SNS or Lambda case, inspect the resource-based invocation permission instead. These are different authorization records even if the same event pattern selects the event, which is why matching alone cannot verify target execution authority.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Event selection and execution permission are separate. SNS and Lambda use resource-based invocation permissions in this brief, so assuming every target uses an execution role misstates the authorization model.

video_need.reason: The choice between execution-role and resource-based target permission models benefits from a rule-to-target authorization diagram.

teaching_notes: Use supplied targets and least-privilege permissions; do not invent target operations.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A managed Config rule is present, but the operator still needs to verify its scope, parameters and actual evaluation results. Rule existence is setup evidence, not the compliance result for every resource.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A Config managed rule evaluates supported resource configuration against the rule’s criteria and configured parameters.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Choose the supplied rule, resource scope and parameters, run or inspect its evaluation, and compare compliant and noncompliant sample resources.

Read each evaluation’s resource ID and compliance result rather than treating the presence of the rule as proof that all resources passed.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Choose the supplied rule and configure its approved resource scope and parameters. Run or inspect evaluation and compare the supplied compliant and noncompliant sample resources. For each sample, record the resource ID and compliance result, then relate that result to the rule criteria. If a noncompliant sample is still reported as compliant, inspect the chosen scope and parameters against the supplied requirement rather than accepting the presence of the rule as success. This example checks automated configuration evaluation; it does not install a remediation workflow or assume that a compliance report establishes malicious activity.

Use the two supplied sample results as a boundary check, not just a success example. One compliant result establishes that the intended acceptable configuration can pass; the noncompliant sample checks that the prohibited configuration is reported. If a sample is outside the configured scope, its result cannot validate the intended in-scope criterion. Tie each inspected resource ID to the configured rule scope and parameters.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A configured rule does not mean all resources passed. Read individual evaluation resource IDs and compliance results. The rule evaluates supported configuration against its criteria and parameters; the actual results must be checked.

video_need.reason: Rule scope, parameters and individual compliant/noncompliant results benefit from one controlled configuration evaluation demonstration.

teaching_notes: Do not add remediation behavior to a detection-only rule task.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An approved cost threshold should alert a named recipient. Configure the budget scope and notification deliberately, and do not describe an alert as an automatic resource stop.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An AWS budget compares cost or usage with a configured budget amount over a selected period.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Create a cost budget with the approved scope, amount and period, then configure an actual or forecast threshold and approved notification recipient.

A notification alerts its recipients; stopping resources requires separately configured actions rather than the notification itself.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Use the approved period, amount and scope for the cost budget. Choose the supplied actual or forecast threshold and approved notification recipient. Compare the configuration with those supplied inputs and retain the recipient setting. The budget compares cost or usage with an amount over a period; the notification alerts recipients. Any resource-stopping action would need separate configuration and is not part of this notification example.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A budget notification does not itself stop resources. It alerts recipients; separately configured actions are required for stopping behavior. Do not imply that notification setup caps the workload's spending.

video_need.reason: A short budget-settings walkthrough helps locate period, scope and recipient settings; text suffices to distinguish alerts from actions.

teaching_notes: Use supplied amounts and thresholds; do not estimate workload cost or configure unrequested budget actions.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied application's commands produce an output that CodeBuild must export. Read the buildspec as both a phase-command plan and an artifact-selection plan, then compare it with the build evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A buildspec is a YAML document describing build commands and artifacts; version: 0.2 supports commands in the same shell environment.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Place supplied commands under phases such as install, pre_build, build and post_build, using commands lists in the needed phases.

Set artifacts.files and, if needed, base-directory to match the generated output, then inspect the build’s phase logs and exported artifact.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Use version: 0.2 in the supplied YAML buildspec. Place the supplied commands in commands lists under the needed phases, such as install, pre_build, build and post_build. Version 0.2 supports commands in the same shell environment. Set artifacts.files, and base-directory if needed, to match the generated output. In the resulting build, inspect each phase's logs and the exported artifact. Suppose the commands succeed but the selected artifact path does not match the generated file: that result does not verify the intended output was exported. Keep command execution and artifact selection visible together rather than treating a build completion label as the entire delivery check.

Compare the file generated by the supplied build command with the artifact selection literally. If the output is under the supplied base directory, artifacts.files must select it from that intended location. Phase logs tell you whether commands ran successfully; exported-artifact inspection tells you whether the release output was retained. A passing command cannot correct an unrelated path selection simply by finishing the build.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Command success and correct artifact export are not interchangeable. The buildspec describes both, and the task verifies phase logs and the exported output. Do not add unfamiliar build commands simply to fill every possible phase.

video_need.reason: Phase commands, artifact path selection and actual phase/output evidence benefit from an annotated buildspec execution demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied commands and application output; require shared shell/testing preparation.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An approved EC2 application revision has deployment file mappings and lifecycle hooks. Connect the deployment group and AppSpec to the intended targets, then inspect what happened on those targets.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: For EC2 deployments, appspec.yml maps revision files to destinations and lists scripts for deployment lifecycle hooks.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Configure the supplied application and deployment group to identify the intended EC2 targets and revision, with the approved service role and installed agent.

Inspect the AppSpec files mapping and hooks, execute the supplied deployment action and verify hook results and application files on the target.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect the supplied appspec.yml files mapping and listed lifecycle-hook scripts. Confirm the approved application, deployment group, intended EC2 targets, revision, service role and installed agent. Execute the supplied deployment action and inspect hook results. Then verify application files on the target against the expected mapping. If the action was requested but a hook failed or files are not as expected, retain that evidence rather than declaring deployment complete. This exercise uses supplied hook scripts and target setup; it does not ask for independent Bash authoring or a new application installation strategy.

Trace one supplied source/destination mapping from AppSpec to the files inspected on the intended target. Then relate a hook outcome to that same deployment revision. A successful hook from another deployment is not evidence for this revision. Keeping revision, target and hook/file results together avoids confusing a configured action with a verified target change, while staying within the provided scripts and installation mappings.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A deployment-action request is not the target verification. AppSpec maps files and lists hooks, while hook results and target files show whether the supplied revision was applied as expected. The approved role and installed agent are part of the supplied setup.

video_need.reason: AppSpec mappings, lifecycle-hook outcomes and target files benefit from a controlled supplied EC2 application deployment demonstration.

teaching_notes: Do not invent lifecycle ordering or hook script behavior beyond the supplied AppSpec facts.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A bounded load test should demonstrate EC2 Auto Scaling behavior within an approved group's limits. Keep the target metric, warmup and capacity settings beside the observed scaling activity.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Target tracking adjusts Auto Scaling capacity to keep a chosen metric near its target value.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Select the approved metric and target value and configure instance warmup along with the group’s minimum, desired and maximum capacities.

Run the bounded load test and compare metric values and scaling activities with resulting capacity; capacity cannot exceed the group’s configured maximum.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Select the approved metric and target value for target tracking. Configure the supplied warmup and minimum, desired and maximum group capacities. During the bounded test, compare the metric values, scaling activities and resulting capacity. If capacity reaches the configured maximum, do not expect the group to exceed it merely because the metric is still above target. The evidence checks how this policy and these bounds behaved in the approved test.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Target tracking does not promise unlimited capacity. It adjusts capacity toward the metric target within the configured group limits. Read scaling activity and resulting capacity, not just the policy's existence.

video_need.reason: A bounded metric/capacity timeline helps show target tracking within limits; the configuration and observation checks remain complete in text.

teaching_notes: Cover EC2 Auto Scaling only; defer load-driven ECS scaling and serverless/database capacity choices.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An ECR repository needs separate approved publisher and consumer access. Check repository operations and the identity-side authentication requirement rather than assuming one policy covers both.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An ECR repository policy grants specified principals repository operations such as pulling images or uploading image layers.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Scope the supplied policy’s principals and actions to approved publishers and consumers, then test push and pull and an unapproved principal.

ECR authentication also requires ecr:GetAuthorizationToken through an identity policy; repository permissions alone do not grant that action.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Scope the supplied repository policy to approved principals and push/pull operations. Test push under the publisher, pull under the consumer and the supplied unapproved-principal case. Also inspect ecr:GetAuthorizationToken in the identity policy, because repository permissions alone do not grant that authentication action. Keep the policy scopes and test identities with the observed results.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Repository permissions alone do not grant ecr:GetAuthorizationToken. Authentication requires that action through an identity policy, while the repository policy covers the specified repository operations.

video_need.reason: A short publisher/consumer policy walkthrough helps distinguish repository actions from identity-side authentication permission.

teaching_notes: Use supplied publisher/consumer roles; do not broaden repository scope to fix an unexplained denial.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Repository cleanup could remove an image version still needed for deployment or rollback. Preview the supplied ECR lifecycle policy against exact digests before applying it.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: ECR lifecycle policies select images using criteria such as tag status and count or age and expire matching images.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use rulePriority, selection and action fields to express the supplied retention policy and run a lifecycle preview before applying it.

Check previewed digests against deployed versions; exclude still-needed versions from eligible expiry rather than assuming deployment makes an image immune to lifecycle rules.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Express the approved retention selection with rulePriority, selection and action fields. Run the lifecycle preview and compare every previewed digest with the supplied deployed-version record. If a still-needed digest is eligible for expiry, exclude that needed version from the eligible selection before applying the approved policy. Keep the preview evidence with the retention decision rather than assuming a deployment reference protects the image.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Deployment does not make an image immune to lifecycle rules. Check previewed digests against needed versions; count, age and tag-status selection can still make an image eligible for expiry.

video_need.reason: A previewed-digest table helps compare retention selection with deployed versions; text fully specifies the preview-before-apply decision.

teaching_notes: Do not invent lifecycle-policy JSON or retention durations; use supplied policy criteria.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An Application Load Balancer endpoint must route requests to the intended backend and judge target health with the intended check. Connect the listener, forwarding rule, target settings and health evidence before concluding that the path works.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An Application Load Balancer listener evaluates routing rules and forwards matching requests to a target group.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Configure the supplied listener protocol and port, forwarding rule and registered target protocol/port, then test the endpoint.

Configure the health-check path, port and success codes to match the backend and inspect target health reasons when a request path fails.

An ALB normally routes to healthy registered targets, but when every registered target in a target group is unhealthy it fails open and routes to those unhealthy targets.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Configure the supplied listener protocol and port, its forwarding rule, and the registered target protocol and port. Test the endpoint. If the path fails, compare the health-check path, port and success codes with the supplied backend requirement and inspect target health reasons. Suppose the health-check path is not the one the backend expects; use that evidence for the approved correction rather than changing unrelated settings. Keep the all-unhealthy case explicit: an ALB normally routes to healthy registered targets, but fails open to unhealthy targets when every registered target in a target group is unhealthy. Do not infer from an unhealthy result alone that no requests can be routed.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: An unhealthy target label is not an unconditional no-traffic guarantee. The all-registered-targets-unhealthy case fails open. Keep that exception beside the normal healthy-target routing rule, and diagnose the supplied path using health reasons and backend settings.

video_need.reason: Listener-to-target traffic, health reasons and the all-unhealthy fails-open exception benefit strongly from a connection-path diagram.

teaching_notes: Preserve fails-open exception; do not introduce unsupported load-balancer algorithm or DNS behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A log group needs the approved retention interval. Verify the configured policy without expecting expired events to disappear physically at the exact expiry moment.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: CloudWatch log-group retention controls how long events remain; by default logs are retained indefinitely.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Set the supplied retention interval with put-retention-policy and inspect the log group’s retentionInDays.

Expired events are marked for deletion; physical deletion typically takes up to 72 hours, so expiry is not necessarily immediate disappearance.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Set the supplied interval with put-retention-policy and inspect retentionInDays on the intended log group. Compare that value with the requirement. Events that expire are marked for deletion, and physical deletion typically takes up to 72 hours. If an expired event remains visible immediately after expiry, keep that delay in the interpretation instead of assuming the retention setting is absent.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Retention expiry and physical deletion are not necessarily simultaneous. Logs are retained indefinitely by default; after a retention policy is set, expired events are marked for deletion, which typically takes up to 72 hours.

video_need.reason: A short retention-setting inspection helps locate retentionInDays, while the text covers indefinite default and physical-deletion delay.

teaching_notes: Preserve typically; do not promise a hard deletion deadline beyond the brief.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A database snapshot should support a verified restoration, not merely appear in a backup list. Follow the intended source snapshot into a separate restored instance and inspect its data marker.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An RDS DB snapshot captures the database instance for later restoration.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Create a manual snapshot for the intended DB instance and wait until its snapshot status is available.

Restore the snapshot to a new DB instance identifier using the supplied network settings; restoration creates a separate instance rather than overwriting the source.

Wait for the restored instance to become available, connect to its endpoint and run the supplied query to verify the recovery marker.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Create the manual snapshot for the supplied DB instance and wait until the snapshot is available. Restore it with a new DB instance identifier and the supplied network settings. Wait for the restored instance to become available, then connect to that instance's endpoint and run the supplied recovery-marker query. Record the source, snapshot and restored identifier together. The restore creates a separate instance; it does not overwrite the original database.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: An available snapshot is not the entire recovery verification. Restoration creates a separate instance, and the supplied query checks its marker after availability. Do not accidentally test the source endpoint and label that as restored-data evidence.

video_need.reason: The available-snapshot-to-separate-restored-instance transition and endpoint marker check benefit from a continuous recovery demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied network settings and query; do not author new SQL or database backup policy.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A reader needs approved access to a particular log group. Collection settings do not grant that reader access, so test authorization under the intended identities.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: CloudWatch Logs uses IAM policies to authorize log-group and log-stream operations.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Grant the approved reader the required read actions on the intended log-group resources and remove unnecessary broader grants; some operations require resource scope *.

Test the approved and unapproved principals against the intended read operations because collecting logs does not itself grant reader access.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Grant the supplied reader the required read actions on the intended resources and remove unnecessary broader grants. Preserve the qualification that some operations require resource scope *. Test the intended read operations under the approved and unapproved principals. Record action, resource scope and identity with each result so the test demonstrates the requested access boundary rather than the collector's ability to write logs.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Collecting logs does not itself grant reader access. CloudWatch Logs authorization uses IAM policies, and some operations need resource scope *. Do not force a narrower unsupported scope just to make the policy look uniform.

video_need.reason: A short read-policy/test comparison helps locate principal and resource scope; the authorization boundary is fully described in text.

teaching_notes: Use supplied read actions and supported scopes; do not invent action-to-resource support rules.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied image needs an ECS task definition with the approved runtime settings. Registration describes the task; running and inspection check the actual task instance.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An ECS task definition specifies the image and container runtime settings for tasks.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Set containerDefinitions entries with name, image, portMappings, cpu and memory settings appropriate to the supplied launch type, and register the task definition.

Run the registered task definition with the supplied cluster and network configuration, then inspect task status and container details to verify the image and runtime settings.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Set the supplied containerDefinitions name, image, portMappings, cpu and memory appropriate to the exercise's launch type. Register the task definition and run it using the supplied cluster and network configuration. Inspect task status and container details, comparing image and runtime settings with the supplied specification. Keep the registered definition and observed task evidence connected instead of checking only that a task-definition revision exists.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A registered task definition is a specification, not proof that a task ran with the intended settings. Inspect task status and container details after the supplied run; do not generalize cpu/memory settings across launch types.

video_need.reason: A short task-definition-to-task inspection helps compare runtime settings, while the bounded configuration procedure is explicit in text.

teaching_notes: Use supplied launch-type settings; defer service desired-count and rollout operation.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An AWS request was denied even though one policy appears to allow it. Diagnose the specific request and applicable constraints before widening permissions. The principal, action, resource and context are the starting evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An access-denied diagnosis is specific to the requesting principal, operation, resource and request context.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect the request and applicable policies for an explicit deny, missing allow or unsatisfied condition and use available denial context to localize the cause.

Resource policies, session policies, permissions boundaries and organization policies can constrain access beyond one identity policy; explicit deny takes precedence.

Make the smallest approved policy or request correction supported by the evidence and retest the denied operation.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Take the supplied denied request and write down the requesting identity, operation, target and context. Compare them with applicable policy statements and any available denial context. Locate an explicit deny, a missing applicable allow or an unsatisfied condition supported by the evidence. Do not stop after finding an allow in one identity policy: resource policies, session policies, permissions boundaries and organization policies can also constrain access. An applicable explicit deny takes precedence. Make the smallest approved request or policy correction and repeat the same operation as the test. Keep the before-and-after evidence specific to this request rather than claiming the corrected identity now has unrestricted access.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: An access denial is not proof that the identity policy merely needs a broader Allow. Other policy constraints may apply, and explicit deny takes precedence. Use the request and denial evidence to choose a minimal approved correction, then retest that operation.

video_need.reason: Following a denied request across applicable constraints and a minimal retest correction benefits from an evidence-led evaluation diagram.

teaching_notes: Do not prescribe broad administrator grants or invent missing policies; follow supplied evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An approved saved Terraform plan is ready to provision an EC2 instance. Execution must use that reviewed plan, and the resulting resource must be compared with it. Do not silently replace the review with a fresh unplanned apply.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: terraform apply PLAN_FILE executes the changes recorded in a saved plan without generating a new plan or prompting for approval.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the supplied approved saved plan file rather than an unplanned apply, and retain the apply outcome as execution evidence.

Inspect terraform show PLAN_FILE and the resulting resource or outputs to check that the created EC2 instance matches the approved plan.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Inspect the supplied file with terraform show PLAN_FILE and identify its planned EC2 settings. Execute terraform apply PLAN_FILE for that approved file and retain the apply outcome. This command executes the saved changes without generating a new plan or prompting for approval, so approval must be the supplied approval of that plan, not an expectation of a later prompt. Inspect the resulting resource or outputs and compare them with the plan. For an example instance, record its actual identity and settings against the planned AMI, instance type and placement supported by the exercise. Execution completion and resource comparison are distinct evidence that together show the reviewed changes were applied as intended.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A saved-plan apply does not generate a new plan or ask for approval. Use the supplied approved file and retain execution evidence; do not rely on a prompt to make the approval decision. Verify the created instance against that plan.

video_need.reason: Saved-plan inspection, execution and live-instance verification benefit from a continuous approved-plan demonstration.

teaching_notes: Apply only the approved saved plan; do not add unplanned mutation commands.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied Systems Manager document should run only on approved managed nodes. The response record needs exact targets and individual invocation outcomes, not just a parent command summary.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Run Command executes Systems Manager documents on managed nodes under authorized access.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use send-command with the supplied document and explicit approved --instance-ids or tag-based --targets and document parameters.

Record the command ID and inspect each invocation’s status and output; the parent command status does not replace per-node result checks.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Use send-command with the approved document, parameters and explicit --instance-ids or supplied tag-based --targets. Record the returned command ID. Inspect each invocation's status and output for the approved target set. Suppose two node invocations succeeded and one failed: preserve those separate results with their target identities rather than describing the entire fleet as successful. The parent command status does not replace the per-node checks. The task executes the supplied document under authorized access; it does not ask for new shell logic or an independently authored fleet document. Keep the scope evidence alongside the results so follow-up can be tied to the actual nodes operated on.

Compare the invocation target IDs with the approved target set before interpreting outcomes. An invocation on an unintended node is a scope discrepancy even if it succeeded. Conversely, a missing or unresolved approved invocation is not success merely because other nodes completed. Record the command ID as the shared execution reference and each target's status/output as its individual operational evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: One command can have different invocation outcomes across nodes. A parent status is not a substitute for per-node status and output. Also, a supplied document does not remove the requirement for explicit approved targets and authorized access.

video_need.reason: One parent command and differing target invocation outcomes benefit from a scoped fleet execution demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied document and parameters; require shared Linux/shell preparation for dependent fleet tasks.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A pipeline should stop an invalid Terraform declaration before the approved apply stage. Use static validation as a gate while keeping its limits clear.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: terraform validate checks configuration syntax and internal consistency without checking remote service state or provider API success.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Initialize needed providers and modules with terraform init -backend=false before static validation where backend access is not needed.

Run terraform validate as a blocking workflow step; stop on its nonzero exit result, correct the invalid declaration and rerun before the supplied approved apply step.

terraform fmt -check checks canonical formatting and can be used as an additional blocking configuration check.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Where backend access is unnecessary, initialize the needed providers and modules with terraform init -backend=false. Run terraform validate as a blocking step. For the supplied invalid declaration, inspect the nonzero result, correct the declaration and rerun validation before the approved apply step. terraform fmt -check can provide an additional blocking formatting check. Record which gate failed instead of calling a syntax result a remote-service result.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Static validation does not verify remote state or provider API success. Formatting checks canonical format, not the full validity or deployability of the infrastructure. Use each check for its stated scope.

video_need.reason: A short invalid-to-valid declaration demonstration helps interpret blocking validation/formatting results without implying API verification.

teaching_notes: Use supplied workflow and corrections; do not imply validation guarantees successful apply.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied AWS automation call encounters an error. The program needs a finite retry budget for eligible errors and useful terminal reporting, not an unbounded loop that repeats every failure.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: AWS SDK retries cover selected transient or throttling errors rather than making every failed request safe to repeat.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Set botocore.config.Config(retries={"mode": "standard", "total_max_attempts": APPROVED_ATTEMPTS}) on the supplied Boto3 client to bound requests with the SDK’s backoff; do not wrap terminal errors in an unbounded retry loop.

Catch botocore.exceptions.ClientError around the supplied call, inspect its response["Error"]["Code"] and response["Error"]["Message"] and preserve response["ResponseMetadata"]["RequestId"] when present; report the terminal failure or exhausted retry outcome.

When configuring Boto3, total_max_attempts includes the initial request, whereas max_attempts in a Config object counts retries after the initial request.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Set the supplied Boto3 client's Config retries to standard mode with total_max_attempts set to the approved finite attempt budget. If the example budget is 3, that includes the initial request and leaves at most two retries. In a Config object, max_attempts instead counts retries after the initial request; using 3 there describes a different budget. Around the supplied call, catch ClientError and inspect Error Code and Message. Preserve ResponseMetadata RequestId when present in the response. Report terminal failure or exhausted retries with that evidence. The SDK retries selected transient or throttling errors with its backoff; this example does not declare every failed request safe to repeat or add a separate unlimited wrapper.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: total_max_attempts and Config max_attempts do not count the same thing. The former includes the first request; the latter counts retries after it. Also, retry support covers selected errors, so a terminal failure must be reported rather than retried indefinitely.

video_need.reason: Initial-request versus retry counting and terminal exception reporting benefit from an annotated bounded-call execution trace.

teaching_notes: Use supplied call and ClientError handling; do not invent error codes, additional retry causes or independent retry loops.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A resource looks unused, but an avoidable-charge claim needs billed cost and usage evidence. Start with the approved account and time interval, then locate the supported driver in the report.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Cost Explorer analyzes billed cost and usage for selected time intervals and grouping dimensions.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Filter the supplied period and account, group by service or usage type, and inspect the cost and usage values to identify the supported cost driver.

Use the billed usage evidence to justify the avoidable charge rather than equating the existence of a resource with a specific charge.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Filter Cost Explorer to the supplied account and period and group by service or usage type. Compare cost and usage values for the suspected driver. Suppose the supplied report attributes a charge to a particular usage type during that interval: cite those values as the reason for the recommendation. Do not assign a numerical charge to a resource merely because it exists. Keep the filtered period, grouping and report values with the conclusion so that the claim is about observed billed usage. This is identifying a supported cost driver, not estimating future workload cost or independently deciding to delete the resource.

Keep billed cost and usage as the basis for the recommendation, not just the apparent resource age or name. If two suspected drivers exist, compare their report categories in the supplied interval before selecting the one the evidence supports. The recommendation should cite the chosen service or usage-type grouping and its values so a reviewer can reproduce the cost attribution without inventing a charge from a resource inventory.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Resource existence is not evidence of a specific billed charge. Cost Explorer analyzes billed cost and usage; use that evidence to justify the avoidable driver. A suspected idle resource is a lead for inspection, not the entire cost conclusion.

video_need.reason: A short billing filter/group walkthrough helps locate actual usage evidence; text suffices for the evidence-versus-resource distinction.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce price estimates or unapproved teardown; use the supplied billing evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
