teaching_blocks.content: A supplied EKS Deployment requests a fixed number of Pods. The lab removes one Pod to test controller reconciliation, so distinguish the removed Pod's lifecycle from the Deployment's requested state.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets to reconcile the requested Pod replicas and Pod template.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Apply the supplied Deployment with kubectl apply -f FILE and inspect kubectl get deployment NAME and the associated Pods.

Delete one controlled test Pod and verify the controller creates a replacement and restores the requested replica count.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Apply the supplied Deployment with kubectl apply -f FILE. Inspect kubectl get deployment NAME and its associated Pods, noting the requested replica count in the exercise. Delete the one approved controlled test Pod through the supplied procedure. Inspect again until the controller creates a replacement and restores the requested count. For an illustrative three-replica workload, the evidence should show the controlled loss and return to the requested three replicas, rather than merely the disappearance of the deleted Pod. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets to reconcile replicas and the Pod template; this exercise does not change load-driven capacity or administer the cluster control plane.

Read requested and observed counts separately during the test. The requested three replicas remain the controller's target; the temporary observed shortage is the controlled condition being reconciled. Completion evidence is the replacement and restored requested count, not the fact that deletion was accepted. Do not describe this task as demand-based scaling, since it preserves a supplied desired count rather than changing it in response to load.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Deleting one test Pod is not changing the Deployment's requested replica count. The controller reconciles the requested Pods and template. Verify replacement and restored count rather than treating the removed Pod's final state as the workload's final state.

video_need.reason: Removing one controlled Pod and observing controller replacement makes desired-replica reconciliation visible over time.

teaching_notes: Use supplied cluster access and deletion procedure; do not add kubectl commands absent from allowed knowledge.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A recovery plan can name all components yet still put them in an unusable order. Build the sequence from supplied dependencies and require evidence that each prerequisite is ready before its dependent work resumes.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A workload recovery plan must account for dependencies and the recovery capabilities needed to satisfy its objectives.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
List the supplied infrastructure, data and service dependencies and place each prerequisite restoration before the steps that depend on it.

Include verification points before dependent services resume so incomplete restoration is not mistaken for usable recovery.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the supplied dependency record says the application needs a restored database and the database needs prepared infrastructure. Put infrastructure restoration before database restoration and database verification before application resumption. These dependencies are example exercise inputs, not a universal AWS recovery sequence. Add the supplied verification point before each dependent service proceeds. If an earlier restoration step is incomplete, the plan should not present its dependent service as ready merely because that later step was scheduled. Compare the complete ordered plan with the stated recovery objectives and capabilities. The useful output is an evidence-checkable dependency order, not an unrelated checklist of resources.

Read each dependency edge as a precondition: a dependent step cannot be considered usable until its prerequisite restoration passes the supplied verification. If independent branches exist in the supplied record, avoid inventing an order between them that the dependencies do not require. The final plan should still make every dependent service's readiness checkpoint explicit and be compared with the stated recovery objectives.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Listing dependencies is not the same as ordering them. Each prerequisite restoration belongs before dependent steps, and verification belongs before dependent services resume. Incomplete restoration must not be treated as usable recovery.

video_need.reason: A dependency graph with readiness checkpoints clarifies why restoration steps must precede dependent services.

teaching_notes: Use supplied dependency graph and objectives; do not invent a mandatory service-wide recovery ordering.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An orders request failed, and structured logs carry the same request identity across relevant events. Query a bounded time window and reconstruct the supplied sequence from that identity and timestamps rather than from unrelated nearby messages.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Logs Insights queries select and transform log events using commands connected with pipe characters.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Select the log group and time window, then use fields @timestamp, @message, REQUEST_FIELD | filter REQUEST_FIELD = "ID" | sort @timestamp asc with the actual supplied request field and identity.

Use shared request identity and event timestamps to reconstruct the supplied symptom’s sequence, retaining the relevant events as evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Select the intended log group and supplied interval. Replace REQUEST_FIELD and ID in the query template with the actual field and request identity from the exercise. The fields command selects timestamp, message and request field; filter keeps the chosen identity; sort orders its events by ascending timestamp. Suppose the matching events show request receipt, a later failure message and a final response record. Retain those events in timestamp order as symptom evidence. That sequence supports correlation of this request; it does not automatically prove every nearby error was its cause. The example uses the stated fields, filter and sort commands without adding aggregation syntax or application tracing.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Time proximity alone does not make two log events part of the same request. Use shared request identity and timestamps together, retain the relevant events, and keep the query scoped to the intended group and time window.

video_need.reason: Querying one request identity and ordering its events benefits from a live structured-log query demonstration.

teaching_notes: Trace the supplied fields/filter/sort query; do not add untaught query functions or X-Ray tracing.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An alarm must reach the operational owner, not merely change state. Set up the approved notification route and verify receipt independently of the alarm's metric evaluation.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An alarm action can publish state-change notifications to an SNS topic without changing the alarm’s metric evaluation.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Configure the approved topic as the alarm’s notification action and create the approved recipient subscription, confirming it when required.

Verify the recipient receives a test alarm notification containing alarm and workload context; a configured but unconfirmed subscription may not deliver notifications.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Configure the approved SNS topic as the alarm action and create the recipient subscription. Confirm it where required. Send the supplied test alarm notification and check that the intended recipient receives alarm and workload context. Retain receipt evidence alongside the subscription configuration. An unconfirmed subscription may not deliver, so configured is not the same as received.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Notification routing does not change the alarm's metric evaluation. A topic action and a recipient subscription need a receipt test; configuration alone, especially an unconfirmed subscription, is not delivery evidence.

video_need.reason: Subscription setup, confirmation where needed and actual notification receipt benefit from a short route verification demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied SNS topic/recipient and test; leave fault injection to its dedicated concept.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied Lambda function performs one bounded operational task. Its execution role must cover that task's approved actions and resources, and invocation evidence must be separated from the operational result.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A Lambda execution role grants the function permission to access AWS resources during invocation.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Assign the approved execution role whose actions and resources are limited to the supplied operational task.

Invoke the function with the supplied payload and inspect its returned result and execution logs, distinguishing successful invocation from a successful operational result.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Assign the approved execution role scoped to the supplied task. Invoke the function with the supplied payload and inspect both the returned result and execution logs. For an illustrative resource check, suppose the invocation succeeds but the returned task result says the expected operation failed. Preserve that distinction instead of describing the task as successful because the function was invoked. The execution role grants access to AWS resources during invocation; it is not an unlimited operating identity. This exercise evaluates the supplied payload and task result, not independent function-feature development or serverless capacity configuration.

For the opposite case, suppose the supplied function returns a task-success result and the execution logs support that outcome. Record both with the approved payload and role context. That verifies this bounded task execution, not every operation the function could conceivably perform. If the task needs an action absent from the approved role, report the permission/result evidence instead of broadening the role during the test.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Successful invocation is not proof of a successful operational outcome. Read the supplied task result and logs under the approved execution role. Keep the role's bounded actions/resources separate from the mere ability to invoke the function.

video_need.reason: Invocation response, execution logs and the operational task result benefit from observing one bounded function execution.

teaching_notes: Use supplied function and payload; do not introduce serverless concurrency or application authoring.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A GuardDuty finding has a severity label, but an operator needs its resource and activity evidence before responding. Use the established investigation path rather than acting destructively from severity alone.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A GuardDuty finding contains a finding type, severity, affected resource and details of suspicious activity.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect resource identity, activity timestamps and finding details, and preserve the evidence supporting investigation.

Follow the established investigation and escalation procedure for the finding type rather than taking destructive action from severity alone.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Open the supplied finding and record its type, severity, affected resource identity and activity timestamps. Inspect the detailed suspicious activity and preserve the supporting evidence. Route the investigation through the established procedure for that finding type. If the finding is severe, include that urgency in the response context, but do not turn it into an unsupported conclusion that the resource is compromised or permission to destroy it. The example teaches bounded finding triage: identify what the finding says, retain the evidence and follow the approved escalation procedure.

A finding timeline should retain the activity timestamps supplied in the finding rather than substituting the time someone opened it. Resource identity narrows which workload the suspicious activity concerns, while type and detail inform the established investigation path. If those details are incomplete, preserve the available evidence and escalate under the procedure. Missing detail is not a basis for asserting an attack mechanism or destroying the resource.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A severity label alone is not the complete investigation or an instruction to take destructive action. Inspect resource identity, timestamps and activity details, preserve the evidence and follow the established finding-type procedure.

video_need.reason: A short finding walkthrough helps locate resource, timestamp and activity evidence while text fully bounds the response decision.

teaching_notes: Do not invent compromise conclusions or specialist incident-containment actions.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Audit objects need approved write and read access without unintended readers. Inspect authorization as its own control, not as an effect of encryption or retention.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: S3 bucket policies can grant or deny object operations to specified principals and resource paths.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Give approved audit writers and readers only their required actions on the intended bucket or object ARNs; inspect other applicable grants and denies.

Test a write and read with approved identities and a read with the unapproved identity; encryption or retention settings do not replace authorization checks.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Scope the supplied bucket policy to the approved writers/readers, required actions and intended bucket or object ARNs. Inspect other applicable grants and denies. Test an approved write, an approved read and an unapproved read, recording the identity and resource path for each. Those results verify the requested access boundary; encryption and retention settings do not replace these tests.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Protected storage settings are not authorization evidence. Even with encryption or retention configured, inspect applicable grants/denies and test approved and unapproved object operations.

video_need.reason: A short approved/unapproved policy-test comparison helps locate audit-object authorization evidence independently of storage controls.

teaching_notes: Use supplied audit paths and policy; do not broaden principal access for convenience.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An audit reader can address an S3 object but still lacks the required KMS authority. Separate object access, key authority and the individual object's encryption metadata before interpreting the read result.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: SSE-KMS encrypts S3 objects with an AWS KMS key, while SSE-S3 uses S3-managed keys.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Reading an SSE-KMS object requires both s3:GetObject permission and kms:Decrypt authority for its key; SSE-S3 does not require KMS key-use permission.

Configure the supplied KMS key as bucket default encryption and test reads with approved object/key authority and with KMS use denied; inspect the object’s encryption metadata.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Configure the supplied KMS key as the bucket's default encryption. For the supplied SSE-KMS object, test a read under approved s3:GetObject and kms:Decrypt authority. Then run the case where KMS use is denied and inspect the result. Read the object's encryption metadata to confirm what applies to that object. Changing bucket default encryption does not re-encrypt existing objects, so a default setting alone is not proof of an older object's encryption. Compare this with the stated SSE-S3 boundary: S3-managed-key encryption does not require KMS key-use permission. Keep those two encryption models distinct in the evidence instead of adding a KMS requirement to every S3 read.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Bucket default encryption does not change the individual encryption of objects that already exist. Inspect object metadata. Also, SSE-KMS read access needs both object permission and KMS Decrypt authority; SSE-S3 does not require KMS key-use permission.

teaching_blocks.title: A boundary that changes the interpretation
teaching_blocks.content: Changing bucket default encryption does not re-encrypt objects that already exist; their individual encryption settings still matter.

video_need.reason: Object permissions, KMS authority and individual encryption metadata form distinct boundaries best clarified with an access-path diagram.

teaching_notes: Keep existing-object/default distinction explicit; do not invent key-policy setup or re-encryption procedures.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A proposed Terraform change can remove infrastructure even when its description sounds like an update. Inspect the saved plan's action types and resource identities before recording a scope-and-impact decision.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A Terraform plan describes proposed additions, updates, deletions and replacements based on configuration, state and observed infrastructure.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Create a saved plan with terraform plan -out=PLAN_FILE and inspect it with terraform show PLAN_FILE; replacement includes destruction and creation, not merely an in-place update.

Compare affected resource identities and every proposed action, including the mandatory deletion case, with the supplied scope and impact criteria and record accept or block with plan evidence; review does not require destructive execution.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Create the saved plan with terraform plan -out=PLAN_FILE and inspect terraform show PLAN_FILE. In the supplied review case, compare each addition, update, deletion and replacement with the approved scope and impact criteria. A replacement includes destruction and creation, not just an in-place edit. Include the mandatory deletion case in the review and record accept or block with the relevant plan evidence. This task does not require destructive execution to demonstrate that a planned deletion was identified. Keep the affected resource identities beside the actions so the decision applies to the actual plan rather than a general opinion that Terraform changes are safe.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Replacement is not merely an in-place update, and review does not require executing a deletion. Inspect every proposed action, including the supplied deletion case, and record the accept/block decision from plan and impact evidence.

video_need.reason: Plan action markers and resource identities benefit from a read-only review demonstration, including deletion and replacement cases.

teaching_notes: Do not execute destructive review cases; keep replacement controls for their later concept.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Before a supplied fleet wrapper may mutate resources, its preview should be compared with the approved targets and actions. Keep wrapper preview separate from the more limited permission check offered by supported EC2 DryRun operations.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: For EC2 API operations that support DryRun, the dry-run request checks permissions without executing the operation; DryRunOperation indicates sufficient permission and UnauthorizedOperation indicates insufficient permission.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the supplied fleet wrapper’s preview mode, inspect its proposed targets and actions and compare them with approved scope without enabling mutation.

Dry-run permission success does not guarantee later operation success or provide a universal preview of every AWS service’s changes.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Run the supplied wrapper's preview mode without enabling mutation. Compare its proposed targets and actions with the approved fleet scope and record any discrepancy. For the supplied EC2 operation that supports DryRun, interpret DryRunOperation as sufficient permission and UnauthorizedOperation as insufficient permission; the dry-run request does not execute that operation. A permission-success result is not a guarantee that a later real operation will succeed. Nor is EC2 DryRun a universal preview of every AWS service's changes. The wrapper's proposed-action evidence and the EC2 permission result address different questions, so retain them separately when deciding whether the supplied task is ready for approval.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: DryRunOperation is permission success for a supported EC2 dry-run request, not proof that a real operation ran. Dry-run permission success also does not guarantee later success or provide a service-wide change preview.

video_need.reason: Wrapper previews and supported EC2 dry-run permission outcomes benefit from a side-by-side nonmutating demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied wrapper preview; do not generalize DryRun to unsupported operations or services.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A fleet command may succeed on some targets and fail on others. Follow-up needs a target-by-target result map so that successful work is not blindly repeated.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A fleet command has separate invocation results for individual targets, which may differ within one command.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect invocation statuses and outputs and record successful, failed and unresolved targets separately.

Use target-specific results to choose the scoped follow-up rather than blindly repeating the entire operation on already successful targets.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
For an illustrative three-target command, inspect each invocation status and output. If node A succeeded, node B failed and node C is unresolved, record those three categories with their target identities. Choose the supplied scoped follow-up using those individual outcomes. Do not label the unresolved node failed without evidence, and do not repeat the entire operation merely because one target failed. The separate invocation results are the basis for follow-up; a single overall command label cannot replace them. Keep the successful targets visible so the next operator can avoid treating the entire fleet as untouched.

The follow-up record should retain what is known and what remains unresolved. For node A, successful output is evidence of completion; for node B, retain the failure evidence; for node C, keep the unresolved status until inspection establishes an outcome. This distinction prevents the next operator from treating uncertainty as permission to repeat a mutation on every target. Use only the supplied scoped follow-up.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Partial failure is not the same as total failure. Successful, failed and unresolved targets need separate records. Use those results for scoped follow-up rather than blindly repeating the operation on already successful targets.

video_need.reason: A per-target success/failure/unresolved result table makes partial fleet outcomes and scoped follow-up substantially clearer.

teaching_notes: Do not invent retry safety or remedial commands; use supplied target-specific follow-up.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An approved session expired while an operational task was being handled. Renew the credentials, but first keep the known outcome of any resource-changing request in view before deciding to retry it.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Temporary credentials stop being usable after expiration and must be replaced with a newly authorized session.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
On an expired-session error, renew the approved session through its credential provider and use the new access key, secret key and token together.

Before retrying a resource-changing operation, inspect its known outcome and use a supported idempotency token where the supplied operation offers one to avoid duplicate effects.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
On the supplied expired-session error, renew through the approved credential provider and use the new access key, secret key and session token together. For a resource-changing request, inspect its known outcome before repeating it. Use a supported idempotency token where the supplied operation offers one. Record whether the original request is known to have taken effect instead of assuming an error always means no effect occurred.

Compare a known completed mutation with an operation whose result is unresolved. Renewed credentials are needed in either case, but the completed mutation should not be described as needing repetition simply because the caller later expired. For the unresolved case, inspect available outcome evidence before retrying and use the supplied operation's supported idempotency token where available. Valid identity and safe repeat behavior are separate questions.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Renewing credentials does not settle a previous operation's outcome. Expired credentials must be replaced, but mutation retries require checking the known result and using supported idempotency where available to avoid duplicate effects.

video_need.reason: A short session-expiry and known-operation-outcome timeline helps explain safe renewal before mutation retry; text covers the rules.

teaching_notes: Do not expose credentials or claim every AWS operation supports idempotency tokens.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An ECS task starts, yet its application still needs AWS permissions. Separate the task execution role's startup work from the task role used by application containers.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The ECS task role supplies credentials for AWS calls made by the application containers.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
The task execution role authorizes ECS startup work such as pulling an image and publishing logs; it is distinct from application AWS permissions.

Set taskRoleArn to the approved least-privilege application role in the task definition and test allowed and denied application operations from the task.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: In the supplied task definition, set taskRoleArn to the approved least-privilege application role. From the task, test the supplied allowed and denied application operations. Inspect those results under the task's application identity. The execution role covers startup work such as image pulling and log publication; those capabilities do not substitute for the application role's permissions.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: The task execution role is not the task role. Successful image pulling or log publication does not establish application AWS access. Set and test the approved taskRoleArn for application calls.

video_need.reason: A simple two-role task diagram helps distinguish startup operations from application calls; text supplies the complete bounded test.

teaching_notes: Do not broaden startup permissions to cover application work; use approved roles.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A sandbox account needs the approved governed baseline. Apply the supplied control configuration, then check each control's actual deployment or evaluation result.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A governed account baseline applies standardized organizational controls and configuration to accounts.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Apply the supplied approved control configuration to the sandbox account and inspect each stated control’s deployment or evaluation result.

Distinguish preventive controls that restrict actions from detective controls that report noncompliance when interpreting the baseline checks.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Use the approved sandbox control configuration and inspect every stated checkpoint. For a supplied preventive control, interpret its result as a restriction on actions. For a supplied detective control, interpret evaluation as reporting noncompliance. Record those different results by control rather than treating all baseline settings as equivalent barriers. The task applies an established baseline; it does not design new organizational security controls.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Preventive and detective controls do different work. A detective noncompliance report is not itself the preventive restriction, and the presence of baseline configuration is not the per-control verification result.

video_need.reason: A short baseline checkpoint walkthrough helps locate preventive deployment and detective evaluation evidence without designing new controls.

teaching_notes: Use supplied approved controls only; do not add organizational-policy behaviors absent from the brief.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied EKS workload needs ordinary configuration and a secret without rebuilding its image or displaying the secret. Select the intended references and test the consumer's safe behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A ConfigMap supplies nonconfidential configuration separately from the container image.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Reference a ConfigMap with envFrom.configMapRef or env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef in the supplied Pod template.

Reference a Secret with env.valueFrom.secretKeyRef or a secret-backed volume and test the consuming workload without printing the secret values.

Secrets require access control and appropriate storage protection; base64 encoding is not encryption.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Reference the supplied ConfigMap through envFrom.configMapRef or env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef in the Pod template. Reference the supplied Secret through env.valueFrom.secretKeyRef or the prepared secret-backed volume. Test the consuming workload without printing secret values. A ConfigMap is for nonconfidential configuration; the Secret still needs access control and storage protection because base64 encoding is not encryption. If the exercise changes a ConfigMap used for environment variables, do not expect values in already-running containers to update automatically. Keep the consumer check tied to the actual supplied configuration and secret references.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Base64 encoding is not encryption. Also, ConfigMap-backed environment variables do not automatically update inside already-running containers after the ConfigMap changes. Test the intended consumer and protect secret values instead of exposing them for inspection.

teaching_blocks.title: A boundary that changes the interpretation
teaching_blocks.content: Environment variables populated from a ConfigMap do not automatically update inside already-running containers when the ConfigMap changes.

video_need.reason: Pod-template references and consumer behavior, including unchanged running-container environment values, benefit from a configuration demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied configuration/secret objects; avoid secret display and untaught rollout/update procedures.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A source revision must flow through CodePipeline build and deployment actions as the intended artifacts. Map declared input/output names first, then verify action evidence follows that revision.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A pipeline has stages containing actions that pass declared input and output artifacts between source, build and deployment operations.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Configure source output, CodeBuild input/output and CodeDeploy input artifact names so each action receives the intended revision’s output.

The CodePipeline service role requires trust for codepipeline.amazonaws.com and permissions for its actions and artifact access; this service role is not GitHub OIDC federation.

Verify action execution evidence carries the intended source revision through deployment and a failed action prevents normal progression to dependent actions.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Compare the source output artifact name with the CodeBuild input, then its output with the CodeDeploy input. The supplied names must connect the intended revision's output between the actions. Inspect the CodePipeline service role's trust for codepipeline.amazonaws.com and its required action/artifact permissions. This is service-role authority, not GitHub OIDC federation. Run the supplied pipeline case and follow action evidence from the source revision through deployment. In the failure case, check that a failed action prevents normal progression to dependent actions. Keep the revision and artifact names with the execution evidence so that a successful action on a different input is not mistaken for the intended release.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A stage list alone does not establish artifact continuity. Actions pass declared artifacts, and their input/output names must connect correctly. Also, CodePipeline service-role trust is not interchangeable with GitHub OIDC trust.

video_need.reason: Revision-specific artifact links, action dependencies and CodePipeline service authority benefit from a pipeline-flow diagram.

teaching_notes: Use supplied action structure and roles; do not introduce Jenkins/GitLab or independent application builds.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: The same approved S3 environment template must be deployed to several bounded account/Region targets. Verify each target's assumed caller and live stack identity rather than assuming the first successful deployment covers the rest.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The same CloudFormation template can provision equivalent resource declarations in multiple approved target environments.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
For each approved account/Region pair, use a named role profile with role_arn and source_profile, verify its caller with aws sts get-caller-identity --profile NAME, and create the supplied stack with that profile and explicit --region REGION.

Inspect stack outputs and S3 bucket identity and location in every intended target and check the supplied unapproved targets received no stack.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: For each supplied approved account/Region pair, use its named role profile configured with role_arn and source_profile. Check get-caller-identity under that profile, then create the supplied stack with the profile and explicit Region. Inspect outputs, bucket identity and bucket location in every intended target. Check that the supplied unapproved targets received no stack. Keep a per-target record instead of one shared success label.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Equivalent declarations are not a single shared deployment result. Verify caller, stack outputs and bucket location in every approved target, and check the unapproved-target boundary separately.

video_need.reason: Repeated explicit-profile deployments benefit from a short per-target identity/output comparison; text fully specifies the bounded checks.

teaching_notes: Deploy the same supplied template; do not design new cross-account infrastructure or target discovery.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An endpoint connection fails, but the symptom does not identify the failing layer. Use the supplied tools and path evidence to localize the issue before making an approved correction.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The subnet’s route table must contain a matching destination route to a usable target for the required network path.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Check DNS resolution and the intended endpoint address using the supplied tools, then inspect route association, required protocol/port rules and response traffic to localize the failing layer.

Network ACLs are stateless, so required requests and responses need permitted traffic in their respective directions.

Make the approved correction supported by the failing layer’s evidence and repeat the endpoint connection test.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Check DNS resolution and the intended endpoint address first with the supplied tools. Inspect the subnet's route-table association and destination route to a usable target, then the required protocol/port rules and response traffic. For a supplied network-ACL case, evaluate requests and responses in their respective directions because ACLs are stateless. If the evidence localizes the failure to a missing response allowance, use the approved correction for that layer rather than altering every control in the path. Repeat the endpoint connection test after correction. This example applies completed external DNS, HTTP/HTTPS and ports/firewall preparation; it does not recreate those foundations or infer a route problem from every connection error.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A permitted request direction is not enough for a stateless network ACL. Required responses need permitted traffic in their direction too. Also, an edited route table is not evidence of the used association; inspect the actual path and retest.

video_need.reason: DNS, actual route association and bidirectional controls form a connection path whose localized failure benefits from layered visual diagnosis.

teaching_notes: Require external networking preparation; do not add command syntax or control behaviors absent from allowed facts.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An established patch task should operate on only the approved managed nodes. Preserve the maintenance-window bounds and inspect per-node compliance afterwards.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Patch Manager uses patch baselines and managed-node targets to scan or install patches and report compliance.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the established maintenance-window task with the approved target set, patch document parameters, concurrency and error limits.

Inspect task execution and per-node patch compliance results to verify which approved instances were patched and which require follow-up.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Use the supplied maintenance-window task, approved targets, patch-document parameters, concurrency and error limits. Inspect execution results and each node's patch compliance result. If one node needs follow-up while others are patched, record that distinction with the target IDs. Patch Manager scans or installs using baselines and reports compliance; the scheduled task alone is not evidence that every approved node was patched.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Task execution is not the full per-node compliance check. Verify which approved instances were patched and which require follow-up, retaining the supplied concurrency and error limits rather than widening the task.

video_need.reason: A short maintenance-window execution and per-node compliance inspection helps locate evidence while text supplies the scope limits.

teaching_notes: Require external Linux package-management and fleet preparation; use established patch tasks only.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A Kubernetes Service should reach the supplied application even as selected Pods change. Connect its selector and port mapping with actual selected endpoints, then test from the supplied client.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A Kubernetes Service provides a stable network endpoint for a changing set of selected Pods.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Set spec.selector to match the intended Pod labels and ports.port and ports.targetPort to map the Service port to the application’s container port.

Apply the supplied Service, inspect its EndpointSlices or endpoints and test the Service address from the supplied client to verify selected Pods receive traffic.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Set spec.selector to match the intended Pod labels and map ports.port to the application's ports.targetPort. Apply the supplied Service and inspect its EndpointSlices or endpoints. Test the Service address from the supplied client to verify traffic reaches the selected Pods. Keep selector, endpoint and client-result evidence together rather than accepting a Service object name as proof of application reachability.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A Service declaration is not the traffic test. Its selector must match the intended Pods, its targetPort must map to the application port, and observed endpoints/client results verify the intended path.

video_need.reason: A Service selector, selected endpoints and port mapping benefit from a request-path diagram and supplied client result.

teaching_notes: Use supplied apply/access procedure; do not introduce cluster networking administration or unsupported Service types.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An alarm is configured, but a controlled failure should demonstrate its behavior and notification path. Bound the experiment before causing the approved sandbox disruption.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Controlled failure experiments test how a system behaves under disruption rather than merely inspecting its configuration.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Define the approved fault, limited scope, expected signals and abort conditions before injecting the sandbox failure.

Observe alarm state history and receipt of the expected notification during the fault, then remove the fault and verify recovery.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Write the supplied fault, limited target scope, expected signals and abort conditions before injection. During the approved fault, observe alarm state history and receipt of the expected notification. Remove the fault and verify recovery using the supplied checks. Keep the observations in sequence: preconditions and limits, injected fault, alarm behavior, recipient receipt and recovery. If the expected notification is absent, preserve that result rather than treating the alarm configuration as proof of a successful test. This is a controlled sandbox experiment, not permission to disrupt production or extend the fault beyond the approved limits.

If the abort condition is reached, follow the approved stop path instead of extending the fault until a desired alarm appears. A test result may show a missed signal, missed notification or unsuccessful recovery, and each should be retained honestly. The experiment's purpose is to verify behavior under a limited planned fault, so staying within scope is part of the result rather than an obstacle to it.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: An alarm's configuration is not demonstrated failure behavior. A controlled experiment verifies state history, actual notification receipt and recovery after fault removal. Define scope and abort conditions before injection, not after a problem appears.

video_need.reason: A bounded injected fault, alarm history, notification receipt and recovery form a changing sequence worth demonstrating together.

teaching_notes: Use approved fault and supplied abort conditions; do not invent failure-injection commands.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied Lambda release uses an alias so the test can target the chosen published version. Keep the immutable version and the movable alias distinct when releasing and rolling back.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A published Lambda version is an immutable snapshot of function code and most configuration.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
A Lambda alias points to a published version and can be updated to direct invocations to a different version.

Use aws lambda publish-version --function-name NAME, then aws lambda update-alias --function-name NAME --name ALIAS --function-version VERSION; invoke NAME:ALIAS through the supplied test and roll back by updating the alias to the approved previous version.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Publish the approved function with aws lambda publish-version --function-name NAME, then update ALIAS to the returned approved VERSION through the stated update-alias command. Invoke NAME:ALIAS through the supplied test and inspect its result. For the controlled rollback, update that alias to the approved previous published version and repeat verification. The version is an immutable snapshot of code and most configuration, while the alias points to a published version and can change that target. Record the alias target before release, after release and after rollback so the test result can be tied to the intended version rather than to an unqualified function name.

Compare invocation targets before and after the alias change. A test against NAME:ALIAS checks the version selected by that alias, whereas an unqualified invocation is not the stated alias test. After rollback, inspect the alias target and repeat the supplied result check for the approved previous version. These observations connect traffic selection with a verified result without claiming the immutable published code was edited.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Changing an alias is not editing a published version. The published snapshot is immutable; rollback here changes the alias's target to an approved previous version. Preserve most configuration rather than claiming the version captures every possible configuration property.

video_need.reason: Published versions remain fixed while an alias moves; a release-and-rollback demonstration makes that changing target visible.

teaching_notes: Use supplied test; do not introduce weighted aliases, concurrency or application code changes.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A managed EKS Deployment needs an approved image update and a controlled rollback case. Follow the template revision and readiness evidence, not just the image-change request.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Changing a Deployment’s Pod template creates a new rollout revision; scaling alone does not create a new template revision.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use kubectl set image deployment/NAME CONTAINER=IMAGE to update the supplied image and kubectl rollout status deployment/NAME to monitor rollout.

On the controlled failure, inspect rollout history and use kubectl rollout undo deployment/NAME --to-revision=REVISION to restore the approved prior revision and verify readiness.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the supplied Deployment and container names in kubectl set image deployment/NAME CONTAINER=IMAGE. Monitor kubectl rollout status deployment/NAME. In the controlled failure, inspect rollout history through the supplied procedure, then use kubectl rollout undo deployment/NAME --to-revision=REVISION for the approved prior revision and verify readiness. A Pod-template change creates a new rollout revision; scaling alone does not create a new template revision. Keep the chosen revision and readiness results with the record so rollback means the verified approved prior template, not an arbitrary change that happens to reduce a symptom.

For the controlled failure, keep the failed rollout's revision evidence and the approved rollback revision separate. The prior revision must be the one the supplied procedure authorizes, not merely the most recent history entry seen by the operator. Readiness after undo is the verification point. A successful undo request cannot substitute for checking whether the restored template's Pods satisfy the supplied readiness result.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Scaling a Deployment is not the same as changing its Pod template and creating a new template revision. For this rollback, restore the approved prior revision and verify readiness rather than treating the undo request as completed recovery.

video_need.reason: Image-template rollout, readiness and return to the approved revision benefit from one controlled EKS rollout demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied cluster access and history/readiness procedure; do not introduce self-managed cluster administration.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A CodeDeploy EC2 blue/green release has replacement instances and an approved traffic-switch point. Keep installation, health evidence, rerouting and rollback verification as distinct stages of the supplied procedure.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An EC2 blue/green deployment installs a revision on replacement instances before rerouting traffic from the original instances.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the supplied blue/green deployment group, replacement fleet and load balancer configuration and verify lifecycle and health evidence before the approved traffic rerouting.

Use the supplied rollback configuration or redeployment procedure and verify traffic and application behavior return to the known-good revision.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the supplied blue/green deployment group, replacement fleet and load balancer configuration. Verify lifecycle and health evidence on the replacement instances before the approved traffic rerouting. For the controlled rollback case, follow the supplied rollback configuration or redeployment procedure and verify traffic and application behavior return to the known-good revision. Record the revision and client-visible behavior with the traffic outcome. This example applies the separate old/new environment arrangement to the supplied EC2 deployment; it does not invent lifecycle-hook ordering, a new fleet or an automatic guarantee of zero disruption.

Use client-visible behavior to verify the traffic outcome after the approved switch and after rollback. Replacement-instance installation evidence is necessary before cutover, but it does not say which fleet clients reach. Conversely, rerouted traffic alone does not establish the expected application revision behaves correctly. Preserve the supplied lifecycle/health evidence, traffic result and known-good behavior check as separate linked observations.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A revision installed on replacement instances is not yet verified traffic cutover. Health and lifecycle evidence precede the approved rerouting, and rollback needs verification of both traffic and application behavior at the known-good revision.

video_need.reason: Replacement-fleet health and old/new traffic rerouting benefit from a blue/green cutover and rollback path diagram.

teaching_notes: Use supplied fleet and rollback procedure; avoid absolute availability promises.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied Python task deliberately fails after creating exercise resources. Cleanup belongs in a finally block and must preserve resources that existed before the exercise.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A Python finally block runs cleanup when control leaves its try block, including when an exception is raised.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use a try block for the supplied failing task and a finally block for the supplied scoped cleanup calls.

Track resources created by the exercise and clean up only those resources, then verify their removal and preservation of preexisting resources.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Wrap the supplied failing task in try and finally using the provided code scaffolding. Put the supplied scoped cleanup calls in finally and track which resource identities this exercise created. When the task raises its controlled exception, verify those exercise resources were removed and the preexisting resources remain. finally runs when control leaves its try block, including when an exception is raised. The cleanup boundary comes from the tracked exercise-created identities, not from deleting every resource that resembles the task's name. This exercise applies supplied task and cleanup calls; it is not independent API authoring or an unbounded account-cleanup script.

Track created identities at the exercise boundary rather than reconstructing ownership from names after failure. A preexisting resource that happens to share a label must remain untouched. When finally runs, its scoped cleanup calls operate on the tracked exercise-created set, and the postcheck verifies both removal and preservation. This is why exception-safe block placement and correct cleanup scope are both required.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Putting cleanup in finally does not make an overbroad cleanup safe. Track only the resources created by the exercise and verify both their removal and preservation of preexisting resources. The block's execution rule does not replace target scoping.

video_need.reason: A short supplied-task exception/cleanup trace helps explain finally and preservation of preexisting resources; text covers the scope rule.

teaching_notes: Require external Python preparation; try/finally ellipses are scaffolding, not a runnable task.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An EC2 setting changed outside Terraform. The next plan should inform an approved choice: restore the declaration or change it to reflect an approved intended setting. Do not confuse updating state with repairing live infrastructure.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Terraform normally refreshes tracked resources before planning, revealing out-of-band changes relevant to the proposed actions.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
After the supplied drift, compare observed instance settings with configuration and decide whether to restore the declaration or update it to reflect an approved intended change.

Generate and inspect a new plan, run the supplied approval/apply workflow and verify live instance settings match the chosen declaration.

A refresh-only plan proposes state and output updates to reflect remote changes; planning alone does not persist them. Applying the approved refresh-only plan persists those updates without changing remote infrastructure to restore configuration.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: After the supplied drift, compare the live instance settings with configuration. Use the approved requirement to decide whether the out-of-band setting should be reversed or accepted by changing the declaration. Generate and inspect a new plan, run the supplied approval/apply workflow and verify the live settings match the chosen declaration. Terraform normally refreshes tracked resources before planning, revealing relevant out-of-band changes. A refresh-only plan proposes state and output updates to reflect remote changes. Applying the approved refresh-only plan persists them without changing remote infrastructure; planning alone does not persist them or restore remote infrastructure to the configuration. Keep the observed drift, chosen intent, planned action and final live comparison in one record so the resolution is evidence-backed rather than simply an updated state file.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Refresh-only is not remote repair. Refresh-only planning proposes state and output updates to reflect remote changes; applying the approved refresh-only plan persists them without changing remote infrastructure. Restoring or accepting an approved setting requires the chosen declaration, reviewed plan, approved workflow and final live-setting verification.

video_need.reason: Live drift, chosen declaration, refreshed plan and final resource comparison benefit from a before-and-after resolution demonstration.

teaching_notes: Preserve normally; do not imply refresh discovers every untracked resource or property.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied Terraform module packages EC2 declarations behind inputs and outputs. Use that interface to inspect the intended instance rather than recreating the module's resources.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A module packages resource declarations behind input variables and output values.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Configure module "NAME" with the supplied source and named input arguments; reference its output as module.NAME.OUTPUT.

Initialize the module, inspect the input values and planned instance settings, apply through the approved workflow and verify the created instance and declared outputs.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Configure module "NAME" with the supplied source and input arguments. Reference its declared output through module.NAME.OUTPUT using the supplied names. Initialize the module and compare inputs and planned instance settings with the approved requirement. Apply through the approved workflow, then verify the created instance and declared outputs. The module packages declarations; its interface does not remove plan review or live verification.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied module is not proof that every input is correct. Inspect input values and planned instance settings before the approved apply, then verify the live instance and outputs.

video_need.reason: A short module-interface walkthrough helps locate inputs and outputs while text fully specifies the supplied-module workflow.

teaching_notes: Use supplied source/interface; do not author a new module or invent output names.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A workload appears lightly utilized, and the exercise asks whether a smaller instance is justified. Rightsizing must preserve performance and capacity requirements, including peak and changing demand.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Rightsizing matches resource type and size to workload performance and capacity requirements rather than simply choosing the smallest instance.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Compare supplied load, utilization and performance evidence with service constraints and recommend a smaller instance only when those constraints remain satisfied.

Account for peak and changing demand in the baseline rather than using one low-utilization sample as sufficient evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Compare the supplied load, utilization and performance baseline with service constraints. Suppose one low-utilization sample suggests spare capacity, but the supplied peak period reaches the required performance boundary. Do not use the low sample alone to justify a smaller instance. A recommendation needs evidence that the proposed size still satisfies the supplied constraints across the relevant baseline. Record the workload requirement, observed baseline and reason to recommend or withhold a reduction. The objective is matching resource type and size to workload needs, not selecting the smallest available instance or inventing a price comparison.

If the supplied baseline supports spare capacity even at relevant peaks, explain how the proposed size still satisfies the stated performance constraint. If evidence is insufficient, withhold the specific reduction and state what the current baseline establishes. That is more defensible than recommending a smaller size from a single low sample. Keep observed load, utilization and performance distinct from the recommendation they support.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Low utilization at one instant is not sufficient rightsizing evidence. Account for peak and changing demand and retain service constraints in the recommendation. Smaller is appropriate only when the supplied performance and capacity requirements remain satisfied.

video_need.reason: A brief baseline/peak/constraint comparison helps evaluate the recommendation; no independent capacity-selection demonstration is needed.

teaching_notes: Use supplied baseline and constraints; do not introduce EC2 pricing estimates or unsupported instance recommendations.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A security finding needs an accountable responder and a usable evidence handoff. Route the finding's actual context rather than replacing it with a stronger claim than the evidence supports.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A finding’s resource identity, severity and activity details provide context needed by the accountable responder.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Route the supplied finding ID or evidence link, affected resource, observed activity and urgency to the responsible owner and apply the established escalation path.

Preserve the finding evidence rather than replacing it with an unsupported claim that the resource is compromised.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Include the supplied finding ID or evidence link, affected resource, observed activity and urgency in the handoff to the responsible owner. Use the established escalation path. Preserve the evidence so the receiving responder can inspect the finding. If the report describes suspicious activity, retain that description rather than declaring the resource compromised without support.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A concise handoff should not erase evidence or exaggerate it. Resource identity, severity and activity details give responder context; an unsupported compromise claim does not replace the finding record.

video_need.reason: A finding evidence handoff is a short document structure; a small context/owner table suffices without a tool demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use established owner and escalation path; do not author specialist security conclusions.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An operational event should reach one approved notification or established Systems Manager action. Pair the tested selection pattern with only the approved target, parameters and permissions.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An EventBridge rule pairs an event pattern with one or more targets to receive matching events.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Set the supplied event bus and pattern and add only the approved SNS or Systems Manager target and required target parameters.

Configure the target’s required permissions, then send matching and nonmatching test events and inspect the approved target’s execution or notification evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Set the supplied event bus and event pattern, then add the approved SNS or Systems Manager target with its required parameters. Configure the target's required authorization model. Send the matching and nonmatching test events and inspect execution or notification evidence at the approved target. Compare the results with the intended rule selection. The setup task is not complete merely because the pattern matches in isolation; the approved target's evidence verifies the route.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A matching pattern is only the selection half of the rule. The approved target, parameters and required permissions are also needed, and positive/negative event tests should be checked against actual target evidence.

video_need.reason: Matched and unmatched events plus actual target evidence benefit from a short established-rule routing demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use established Systems Manager action or approved SNS target; do not author a new response document.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An ECS service should keep a requested number of tasks running. The controlled task-removal test checks service reconciliation, not just the lifecycle of the removed task.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An ECS service maintains the desired number of tasks and replaces tasks that stop or fail.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Create the service with the supplied cluster, task definition, network settings and desiredCount.

Remove one task in the controlled exercise and inspect service events and running/pending task counts until the desired count is restored.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Create the service with the supplied cluster, task definition, network settings and desiredCount. During the exercise, remove the one approved task and inspect service events plus running and pending counts until the requested count is restored. For an example desired count of three, the record should show the controlled loss and restoration to that requested count. The service replaces stopped or failed tasks; the task definition supplies what runs, while the service maintains the desired number.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: The removed task's final state is not the service's desired-state outcome. Inspect replacement behavior, service events and running/pending counts until desiredCount is restored.

video_need.reason: A controlled task loss and return to desiredCount makes ECS service reconciliation visible over time.

teaching_notes: Use supplied removal procedure; defer task identity and rolling deployment details to their own concepts.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A promotion job must require both supplied unit and integration tests. Make failure visible to the workflow and preserve the dependency on both jobs rather than allowing promotion to ignore a failing test.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A nonzero command exit status reports failure to a pipeline step, while zero reports success.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Run the supplied unit and integration test commands in workflow steps with run: TEST_COMMAND; set the promotion job’s needs: [UNIT_JOB, INTEGRATION_JOB] to require both test jobs.

Do not set continue-on-error on the blocking test steps; demonstrate a failing supplied test prevents the dependent promotion.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Run the supplied TEST_COMMAND values in test steps and set the promotion job's needs to the supplied unit and integration job names. Do not set continue-on-error on blocking test steps. Use the seeded failing test and inspect its nonzero exit result and the dependent promotion outcome. Record that the test failure prevents promotion; an independently successful other test is not enough to satisfy both gates.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A command that failed must not be converted into a tolerated blocking-test result with continue-on-error. The promotion dependency requires both test jobs, and the supplied failure case demonstrates that progression is blocked.

video_need.reason: A seeded test failure and blocked dependent promotion benefit from a short workflow execution demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied tests; do not teach application test authoring or unfamiliar shell exit-handling syntax.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A small infrastructure change should be understandable at review and traceable through approved execution. Keep intent, focused diff, saved plan and resource verification in one change record.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Small coherent changes reduce review complexity and make delivery feedback easier to act on.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
In the supplied repository workflow, stage the focused files with git add FILES, commit with git commit -m "MESSAGE", push the review branch with git push, and open its supplied pull-request interface to request review.

Submit a focused infrastructure pull request with its intent, coherent diff and saved plan evidence showing the affected EC2 resource.

After the supplied approval, execute the supplied CI apply using the approved saved plan and attach the execution and resource-verification evidence to the change record.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Stage only the focused supplied files, commit with a descriptive supplied message and push the review branch through the established Git workflow. Open its supplied pull-request interface to request review. Include the change's intent, coherent diff and saved plan evidence for the affected EC2 resource. After supplied approval, run the supplied CI apply with that approved saved plan and attach execution plus resource-verification evidence. The example carries one focused change from review to verified outcome instead of mixing unrelated modifications into the submission.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Review approval alone is not the execution record. Retain the approved saved plan, supplied CI apply outcome and live-resource verification. A small coherent diff improves reviewability but still needs those execution checks.

video_need.reason: A short focused diff/plan/approval/execution record walkthrough helps show traceability, while the bounded review workflow is explicit in text.

teaching_notes: Require external Git/CI preparation; use supplied review interface and approved apply workflow.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A workload has capacity in more than one Availability Zone, but the controlled test must show required client-visible behavior during an approved AZ-component loss. Surviving resources alone do not establish availability.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Resilience testing deliberately introduces failures to verify the workload can meet its availability requirements.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Limit the approved failure to the supplied AZ components, define abort criteria, and monitor client-visible service behavior during the experiment.

Check that the remaining independent capacity and request path maintain the required service behavior rather than inferring availability from surviving instance count alone.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Define the approved AZ-scoped failure and abort criteria before the experiment. During the supplied failure, monitor the client-visible service behavior. Compare the remaining independent capacity and request path with the service requirement. Suppose some instances survive but clients cannot complete the required request: record that the availability criterion was not demonstrated, rather than calling the test passed from the survivor count. Keep the failure scope, observed client behavior and remaining-path evidence together. This is deliberate resilience verification within supplied limits, not an exercise to disable an entire Region or infer availability from the existence of multiple locations.

For a passing result, retain the client check that demonstrates required behavior along with the surviving path and capacity observations. If remaining resources exist but the request path fails, the availability criterion has not been met. These two contrasting cases show why the experiment monitors the service from the client perspective instead of treating resource survival as an automatic availability proof.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A surviving instance count is not a client-visible availability result. Verify that remaining independent capacity and the request path maintain the required behavior, and keep the experiment within the approved AZ components and abort limits.

video_need.reason: An AZ-scoped loss and surviving client request path benefit from a failure-domain diagram tied to observed service behavior.

teaching_notes: Use approved failure procedure; do not introduce regional failover or unsafe production faults.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Exercise teardown should remove only approved resources in dependency order. The operator also needs to inspect what was retained or failed to delete, without claiming deletion completion is billing verification.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Resource deletion must respect dependencies; CloudFormation uses resource relationships when deleting a stack.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Identify only the supplied exercise resources by stack membership or approved tags, remove dependent resources before their prerequisites and verify deletion results.

An S3 bucket must be empty before deletion; remove the exercise bucket’s objects, all object versions and delete markers before deleting that bucket.

Retained resources and failed deletions need explicit inspection and approved follow-up; a completed deletion operation is not billing verification.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Identify exercise resources by approved stack membership or tags. Remove dependents before their prerequisites and verify deletion results. For the supplied S3 bucket, empty objects, all object versions and delete markers before deleting the bucket; a current listing alone is not the stated version cleanup. Inspect any retained resources and failed deletions for approved follow-up. CloudFormation uses resource relationships during stack deletion, but that does not remove the need to inspect retained or failed resources. Keep the scope and per-resource deletion evidence in the cleanup record. A completed deletion operation is not a proof of zero charge: this task verifies resource removal, while the later billing check verifies residual charges.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Deleting a versioned bucket requires emptying versions and delete markers as well as objects. Also, a completed deletion operation is not billing verification. Inspect retained resources and deletion failures rather than assuming every exercise resource disappeared.

video_need.reason: Dependent-first removal, versioned-bucket contents and retained/failed resources benefit from a scoped teardown sequence diagram.

teaching_notes: Use approved scope and dependency order; leave residual-charge verification to its later concept.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Recovery rehearsal needs a valid session that can perform the required work. Check lifetime and authorization independently before using it for restoration.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Recovery execution needs a valid, unexpired session with the permissions required for backup access and resource creation.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Establish the approved recovery session, inspect its identity and expiry, and test the supplied backup-read and recovery-resource operations before rehearsal.

A valid credential lifetime does not prove sufficient authorization; verify both access outcomes and lifetime.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
