teaching_blocks.content: Establish the approved recovery session and inspect its identity and expiry. Test the supplied backup-read and recovery-resource operations. Record both outcomes alongside the credential lifetime. If the credentials are unexpired but the backup-read test is denied, they are not ready for the required recovery. Conversely, permission evidence does not remove the need for a valid session during execution.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Unexpired credentials do not prove sufficient authorization. Recovery readiness needs both valid lifetime and successful required access tests for backup reading and resource creation.

video_need.reason: A short identity/expiry/access check helps distinguish session validity from authorization, while text states both readiness requirements.

teaching_notes: Use approved session provider and safe supplied tests; do not expose credentials.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A recovery rehearsal must stay inside the approved environment. Confirm restoration destinations and test traffic before provisioning resources, not only after clients begin using them.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Recovery testing should use a controlled environment that limits the experiment’s effects.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Prepare the supplied isolated account and network target and check restoration destinations and client test traffic do not point to production.

Record the approved scope and stop conditions before provisioning recovery resources or directing test traffic.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Prepare the supplied isolated account and network target. Inspect restoration destinations and client test traffic settings to confirm they do not point to production. Record approved scope and stop conditions before provisioning or redirecting traffic. Keep those settings beside the rehearsal record so isolation is evidence of the actual targets, not just a label on the exercise.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Calling an account a sandbox is not the complete isolation check. Restoration destinations and client traffic must also stay out of production, and approved scope/stop conditions must be recorded before the experiment acts.

video_need.reason: A short rehearsal-target and client-traffic diagram helps verify isolation without introducing a new environment design.

teaching_notes: Use supplied isolated target; do not create production cutover or new network-isolation design.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A protected Automation operation requires approval and an enforceable stop path. Position that decision before the operation and inspect the actual execution state when stopping.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An aws:approve Automation step pauses execution pending approval or rejection by the designated approvers.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Put the approval step before the protected operation and use the supplied branching or failure path to prevent that operation on rejection or stop.

Stop an Automation execution with the approved stop operation when a stop condition occurs and inspect execution state before allowing further actions.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Place the supplied aws:approve step before the protected action. Use the established branching or failure path so rejection or stop prevents that operation. In the supplied stop-condition test, use the approved stop operation and inspect execution state before allowing further actions. The approval step pauses for designated approvers; it is not authorization to run the protected action before they decide.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: An approval request is not an approval outcome. Rejection or stop must prevent the protected operation, and a stop request still requires inspecting execution state before further action is allowed.

video_need.reason: Approval pause, rejection/stop and protected-action state benefit from a short controlled Automation execution demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied branching and stop operation; do not invent Automation document syntax.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An operational response needs an audit record for successful and failed steps. Connect the Automation execution context with CloudTrail evidence of the underlying AWS actions.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Automation execution details include an execution identifier, step statuses, inputs, outputs and failure information.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Record execution ID, acting role, target identities, start/end times and per-step outcomes for the supplied response.

Use CloudTrail request identity and operation evidence to attribute the underlying AWS actions; success and failure outcomes both belong in the response record.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Record the execution ID, acting role, targets, start/end times and per-step outcomes from the supplied response. Inspect inputs, outputs and failure information as part of that record. Use CloudTrail request identity and operation evidence to attribute the AWS actions. If a step failed, retain its evidence rather than omitting it from a success-focused summary. This makes the record describe what the response actually attempted and achieved.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Audit evidence is not only a list of successful steps. Inputs, outputs, failure information and attributed underlying operations all matter. Keep both success and failure outcomes with the execution identity and targets.

video_need.reason: A short execution-to-CloudTrail evidence walkthrough helps locate step outcomes and attributed operations; text covers the required record.

teaching_notes: Use supplied execution/CloudTrail records; do not infer actions from the operator’s intended plan.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Audit logs need tamper evidence as well as storage controls. CloudTrail digest validation checks the delivered log interval; it does not itself prevent someone from accessing or deleting the files.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: CloudTrail log-file integrity validation uses signed digest files and hashes to detect modification or deletion of delivered log files.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Run aws cloudtrail validate-logs --trail-arn ARN --start-time TIME --end-time TIME --region REGION against the supplied log/digest interval and inspect validation failures; for an organization trail also provide the required --account-id.

Digest validation supplies tamper evidence but does not itself prevent unauthorized access or deletion.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Substitute the supplied trail ARN, start/end times and Region into aws cloudtrail validate-logs. For an organization trail, include the required --account-id for the supplied account. Inspect validation failures for that log/digest interval. The validation uses signed digest files and hashes to detect modification or deletion of delivered logs. Keep the interval and validation result in the evidence record rather than declaring all logs intact from an unrelated successful interval. A passing validation result is tamper-evidence verification for the checked material, not an authorization control or prevention of future deletion.

Keep validation scope explicit in the result: trail identity, account when required, selected interval and Region. A failure is evidence to preserve and investigate under the supplied procedure, not a reason to omit the affected files from the record. Authorization and retention still need their own controls because knowing that material was changed or deleted is not the same as preventing that action.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Digest validation detects tampering; it does not prevent unauthorized access or deletion. Run it on the supplied log/digest interval and preserve failure evidence, keeping that role distinct from access and retention controls.

video_need.reason: Digest validation over a selected interval and its failure evidence benefit from observing the supplied tamper-check operation.

teaching_notes: Include organization-trail account-id where required; do not invent validation output or claim preventive protection.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Audit retention applies to individual object versions, and the selected Object Lock mode changes what bypass is possible. Verify version retention rather than inspecting only the bucket default.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: S3 Object Lock applies retention to object versions using governance or compliance mode and a retain-until date.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Apply the supplied default retention duration and mode on the prepared Object Lock bucket and inspect individual audit-object version retention.

Compliance mode prevents deletion or shortening of retention during the retention period even by root; governance mode permits bypass only with the necessary bypass authorization and request.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: On the prepared Object Lock bucket, apply the supplied default duration and mode. Inspect audit-object version retention and its retain-until date. For compliance mode, deletion or shortening is prevented during that period even by root. For governance mode, bypass requires the necessary bypass authorization and request. Record the mode and version-specific retention rather than describing all Object Lock retention as identical.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Governance and compliance modes have different bypass boundaries. Governance permits authorized requested bypass; compliance does not permit deletion or shortened retention during the period even by root. Check the individual audit-object version.

video_need.reason: A short version/mode/retain-until comparison helps distinguish governance bypass from compliance retention; text covers the rules.

teaching_notes: Use prepared bucket and supplied retention policy; do not create irreversible unapproved compliance settings.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Terraform's remote state bucket must already exist before it can store state for the configuration that manages exercise resources. Keep backend bootstrap, backend selection and migration distinct.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The S3 backend stores Terraform state in a specified bucket and key, separate from the configuration that declares managed resources.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Provision the protected backend bucket with the supplied local-state bootstrap configuration. Substitute the actual supplied bucket, key and Region in the line-separated backend block. The block configures state storage; it is not the resource declaration that creates the bucket. After changing the backend, run terraform init -migrate-state, approve the supplied migration and verify state at the intended bucket/key. Keep the bootstrap result and migrated-state location with the record so the workflow does not assume a backend can create itself before initialization. Apply the supplied protection settings without introducing a new backend design or another storage service.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Backend configuration names an already-provisioned state location; it is separate from managed-resource declarations. Provision the backend bucket first, then initialize/migrate and verify the intended bucket/key rather than treating the HCL block as bucket creation.

video_need.reason: Local bootstrap, backend selection and state migration are distinct transitions best clarified in one HCL-to-state-location demonstration.

teaching_notes: Show line-separated HCL, not comma-separated shorthand; use supplied bootstrap and migrate-state approval.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A replacement plan can have a permitted order or be prevented by a lifecycle rule. These controls affect mechanics, but the operator still needs scope and impact approval for a permitted change.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: By default Terraform destroys an object before creating its replacement; create_before_destroy requests the reverse order where supported.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
prevent_destroy rejects a plan that would destroy the protected resource while that lifecycle rule remains in its configuration.

Set the supplied lifecycle argument in the resource block, introduce the controlled replacement-triggering change, and inspect the plan’s replacement order or prevention error before the approved permitted apply.

Lifecycle settings constrain replacement mechanics but do not replace scope and impact approval.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Set the supplied lifecycle argument in the resource block and introduce the approved controlled replacement-triggering change. Inspect the plan's replacement order or prevention error. By default Terraform destroys the old object before creating its replacement; create_before_destroy requests the reverse where supported. prevent_destroy rejects a destruction plan while that rule remains in configuration. If the plan is permitted, follow the supplied approval before applying it. Record the order or rejection evidence separately from scope/impact authorization. Do not describe a lifecycle setting as a substitute for review or as a guarantee that every replacement can be performed with both objects coexisting.

Compare two approved controlled plans: one requests create-before-destroy where supported, while another destruction is rejected by a still-present prevent_destroy rule. The first record concerns ordering; the second concerns plan prevention. Neither result proves the change's business impact is acceptable. Scope review and approval remain necessary for the permitted plan, while the prevention error is evidence that the configured lifecycle boundary blocked that destruction.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: create_before_destroy is a request for reversed replacement order where supported, not a universal feasibility guarantee. prevent_destroy applies while its rule remains in configuration. Neither lifecycle setting replaces scope and impact approval.

video_need.reason: A planned replacement order or prevention error benefits from comparing controlled lifecycle configurations and their plan evidence.

teaching_notes: Preserve where-supported and rule-remains qualifiers; do not imply protection after configuration removal.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An isolated recovery target needs replacement EC2 infrastructure from a supplied CloudFormation template. Confirm authority, Region and parameters before creation, then verify recovery readiness beyond stack completion.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Creating a stack from a template provisions its declared resources under the target account’s execution authority and selected Region.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the supplied restoration template, approved recovery credentials, explicit isolated target and required parameters to create the replacement EC2 stack.

Monitor stack events until creation completes, inspect resource IDs and outputs, and run the supplied instance and service recovery-ready checks.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Use the approved recovery credentials, explicit isolated account/Region target and required parameters with the supplied restoration template. Monitor stack events until creation completes. Inspect resource IDs and outputs, then run the supplied instance and service recovery-ready checks. If the stack completed but the service check fails, record those separate outcomes. The template provisions declared resources under the target account's execution authority and selected Region; the later checks establish whether the created instance and service are recovery-ready. This exercise does not switch production endpoints or introduce an independently designed restoration template.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Stack creation completion is not the whole recovery-readiness result. Resource IDs/outputs and supplied instance/service checks must be inspected. Keep the explicit isolated target and approved execution authority with the creation evidence.

video_need.reason: Isolated stack creation followed by instance/service readiness checks benefits from one continuous restoration demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied template and checks; do not introduce production cutover or guest-OS authoring.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A release security scan is useful as a gate only when its evidence is compared with an explicit severity threshold and exception policy. The result should control promotion according to that policy.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Inspector findings report vulnerability evidence, affected resources and severity that can inform release decisions.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Compare the supplied scan report with the stated severity threshold and documented exception policy to decide whether a finding is actionable.

Make the scan-policy check return failure for an actionable unexcepted finding and require its success before promotion; retain the report and policy decision as evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Read the supplied Inspector report's affected resource, vulnerability evidence and severity. Compare findings with the stated threshold and documented exceptions. For an actionable unexcepted finding, make the supplied policy check return failure and require success before promotion. Retain the report and the policy decision. If a documented exception applies, record that policy basis rather than silently dropping the finding. This is a bounded release decision using supplied scan evidence, not a lesson in vulnerability exploitation, specialist remediation or inventing a new severity policy.

Compare an actionable unexcepted finding with one covered by a documented exception. Both remain scan evidence; the supplied policy determines their different gate outcomes. Retain the exception basis alongside the finding rather than claiming the scanner did not detect it. If a blocking policy result is tolerated by the workflow, the gate is not enforcing the stated precondition even though the scan ran.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A scan report alone is not an enforced release gate. The policy check must fail for actionable unexcepted findings and promotion must require its success. Also, severity should be read alongside the documented threshold and exception policy.

video_need.reason: A short scan-evidence/policy-outcome walkthrough helps apply the threshold and exceptions; no vulnerability exploitation demonstration is needed.

teaching_notes: Use supplied scan/threshold/exceptions; do not invent vulnerability facts or policy exceptions.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A pipeline has stopped, and several later actions did not run. Start with the first failing action in the selected execution instead of treating every unrun dependent action as an independent failure.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Pipeline execution and action history identify failed actions and their error details.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Find the first failing action in the selected execution, inspect its input artifact revision and linked service logs, and use the error evidence to identify the correction.

Retest after the approved correction and verify that action succeeds before investigating later dependent actions that did not run.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Open the supplied execution and action history. Identify the first failing action, inspect its input artifact revision and follow its linked service logs. Use the error details to select the approved correction. Retest and verify that action succeeds before investigating later dependent actions that did not run. Keep execution and revision identities with the evidence so a successful retry of a different input is not mistaken for correcting this failure. The example follows the pipeline's dependency break and service evidence; it does not guess the cause from the name of a later blocked stage.

If the source action succeeded and the build action failed, start with the build input revision and build logs rather than diagnosing the deployment action that never ran. After the approved correction, verify the same required action can succeed with the intended input. That progression follows the execution's evidence and dependency structure, instead of turning every later unrun action into a separate root cause.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Not run is not the same evidence as failed with an error. Find the first failing action and its input/logs, retest the approved correction and verify success before investigating dependent actions that could not progress.

video_need.reason: Execution history, first failing action, input revision and linked service logs benefit from an evidence-led troubleshooting demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied logs/error evidence; do not invent corrective commands or unsupported causes.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Telemetry shows a workload symptom, but the cause may be in the host, instance software or container. Combine the supplied time window with component inspection before changing anything.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: EC2 system status checks concern underlying AWS host issues, while instance checks concern the instance’s software and networking.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the supplied metric and log time window to identify the affected workload, then inspect the component’s service status, events and logs rather than assuming the symptom proves its cause.

For a container, inspect container state, exit status and recent logs; apply the evidence-supported correction and repeat the supplied health check.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the supplied metric/log interval to locate the affected workload. For EC2, read system status checks as underlying AWS-host evidence and instance checks as instance software/networking evidence. Inspect component service status, events and logs using the prepared Linux skills and supplied procedure. For a container, inspect its state, exit status and recent logs. Select the approved correction supported by that evidence and repeat the supplied health check. If a metric improved but the required health check still fails, retain that outcome rather than declaring recovery from a single signal. The symptom identifies what to investigate; it does not by itself prove the cause.

A component inspection result should be tied to the telemetry interval and affected resource. Logs from another component or time window may not explain this symptom. After the approved correction, compare the repeated supplied health check with the original failure. Keep any remaining failed checks visible; one improved metric or restarted process does not erase the application health criteria the task requires.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: System and instance status checks concern different boundaries. A metric or log symptom is not automatically its own cause. Inspect the component and repeat the supplied health check after an evidence-supported correction.

video_need.reason: Correlating workload telemetry with component state and repeated health checks benefits from a controlled diagnostic demonstration.

teaching_notes: Require external Linux service/process preparation; do not author new inspection commands or boot-startup configuration.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Deployment completion must be followed by a live smoke check for the intended revision. The validation action should report success to CodePipeline only after the supplied behavior check passes.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A post-deployment validation action checks live application behavior rather than merely whether a deployment operation completed.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Run the supplied smoke-check action against the deployed endpoint and verify the expected response for the deployed revision.

In the supplied Lambda validation action, call CodePipeline PutJobSuccessResult with the job ID only after a passing smoke check; call PutJobFailureResult on failure so dependent progression remains blocked.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Run the supplied smoke-check action against the deployed endpoint and compare its response with the expected response for that revision. In the supplied Lambda validation action, send PutJobSuccessResult with the job ID only for a passing check. For failure, send PutJobFailureResult so dependent progression remains blocked. Keep the revision, endpoint result and reported job outcome in the evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A completed deployment operation is not a live application check. The smoke test validates behavior, and its passing result must precede PutJobSuccessResult. Report failure rather than advancing dependent progression when the supplied check fails.

video_need.reason: Live smoke response and success/failure reporting to the dependent pipeline benefit from a short validation-action demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied smoke action/Lambda scaffolding; do not teach application endpoint test authoring.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An event reaches a target that cannot accept it. Configure a finite retry budget and failure capture so the supplied delivery failure can be inspected instead of disappearing into indefinite retries.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: EventBridge retries retryable target-delivery failures within configured maximum event age and retry-attempt limits.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Configure the target RetryPolicy MaximumRetryAttempts and MaximumEventAgeInSeconds to the approved finite budget.

Configure DeadLetterConfig with the approved SQS queue ARN and required queue permissions, then inspect a seeded exhausted delivery failure in that queue.

Some nonretryable delivery failures go directly to failure capture; retry configuration does not guarantee every failure receives retries.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Set RetryPolicy MaximumRetryAttempts and MaximumEventAgeInSeconds to the approved finite limits. Configure DeadLetterConfig with the approved SQS queue ARN and required queue permissions. Inspect the seeded exhausted-delivery failure in that queue and retain its evidence. Retryable target-delivery failures are retried within both age and attempt limits. Some nonretryable failures go directly to capture, so do not expect every failure to exhibit the full retry sequence. The example verifies the bounded policy and captured failure together; merely configuring a retry count does not prove that the capture queue can accept or holds the supplied failed event.

Compare the supplied retryable-exhaustion case with a captured nonretryable failure. The first should be interpreted against finite age and attempt limits; the latter need not show a full retry history. Both require inspectable capture evidence at the approved queue. Required queue permissions are part of that route, so a configured ARN alone cannot be substituted for the actual captured-event check.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Retry configuration does not guarantee that every failure receives retries. Some nonretryable failures go directly to capture. Also, a configured dead-letter queue requires the required permissions and inspection of the seeded failure to verify capture.

video_need.reason: Finite retry attempts, event age and captured delivery failures benefit from a delivery timeline with the nonretryable branch shown.

teaching_notes: Use supplied finite limits and SQS queue; do not invent retry intervals or guaranteed retry causes.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An ECS service needs a new image revision without treating the update request as proof of a healthy rollout. Read the supplied replacement bounds and observe service/task health until steady-state criteria pass.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An ECS rolling deployment replaces service tasks according to minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent relative to desiredCount.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Register the supplied new image version in a task-definition revision and update the service to that revision.

Inspect service events, running task revisions and health until the supplied steady-state criteria are met; a service-update request alone is not proof of a healthy rollout.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Register the supplied new image in a task-definition revision and update the service to it. Inspect service events, running task revisions and health against the supplied criteria. minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent describe replacement bounds relative to desiredCount. Keep those settings with the observations rather than assuming every rolling update replaces all tasks at once. Stop calling the rollout complete at the update request; verify the supplied steady state.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Service-update acceptance is not a healthy rollout result. Verify events, running revisions and health until the supplied steady-state criteria are met, using the configured percent bounds relative to desiredCount.

video_need.reason: Changing task revisions, replacement bounds and eventual steady-state health benefit from a short ECS service rollout demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied task definition and steady-state checks; do not add load-driven ECS scaling.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A staging-tested release should promote the same built content to the next environment. Change the supplied environment configuration without rebuilding the source into a different output.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The build stage produces a build artifact; release combines that build with environment configuration, and run executes the release.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Promote the same immutable artifact reference or digest to the next environment while supplying that environment’s configuration rather than rebuilding the source.

Compare the deployed artifact digests in staging and production and their recorded build provenance to verify the tested output is the promoted output.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Carry the same immutable artifact reference or digest from staging to production and supply production's approved configuration. Compare deployed digests in both environments and their recorded build provenance. If the digests differ, the evidence does not show that the tested output was promoted. Build produces the artifact, release combines it with environment configuration, and run executes that release.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Rebuilding from the same source is not this same-artifact promotion check. Promote the immutable reference/digest and verify deployed digests with build provenance; environment configuration belongs to the release combination.

video_need.reason: A short environment/digest/provenance comparison helps verify same-content promotion without a new build demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use supplied artifact and environment configuration; do not create a new build during promotion.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Teardown removed resources, but the bill still needs a time-aware check. Cost Explorer may report older usage after deletion, and an absence of resources is not a zero-cost result.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Cost Explorer data is refreshed at least once every 24 hours and some data can take longer to appear.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect the supplied teardown interval with account and service or usage-type filters and compare usage timestamps with resource-deletion evidence.

Distinguish charges for usage before deletion from evidence of continuing usage and repeat the check after the billing data refresh rather than declaring zero cost from resource absence.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Filter the supplied teardown interval by account and service or usage type. Compare usage timestamps with resource-deletion evidence. A charge associated with usage before deletion is different from evidence of continuing usage after deletion. Record that timing distinction and repeat the check after the billing-data refresh. Cost Explorer refreshes at least once every 24 hours, and some data can take longer to appear. Do not declare zero cost solely because the resources are gone or the first post-teardown report is empty. This exercise verifies residual charges against deletion evidence and reporting delay rather than inventing a new price estimate.

If the first report has no charge in the teardown interval, retain that observation but label it as the current reporting result. Repeat after refresh before concluding about residual charges. If a later report adds usage, compare its usage timestamps with deletion evidence rather than assuming its appearance time is its usage time. This makes the conclusion about metered activity and reporting lag, not the time the operator opened the report.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A charge appearing after deletion is not automatically proof of post-deletion usage. Compare usage timestamps and repeat after data refresh. Conversely, resource absence or an early empty report does not prove zero cost.

video_need.reason: A short usage-time/deletion-time comparison helps distinguish residual reporting from continuing usage; the billing-delay rules suffice in text.

teaching_notes: Preserve at-least-daily refresh and possible longer appearance delay; do not promise a fixed final billing time.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Remote Terraform state can contain sensitive values, so its reader/writer boundary needs its own access test. Backend access isolation is different from coordinating concurrent authorized writers.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: S3 backend access needs permissions for the selected state bucket and object key; state can contain sensitive values.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Scope approved readers and writers to the required ListBucket prefix and GetObject/PutObject state object operations, with supplied locking permissions configured separately.

Initialize the supplied backend, provision the separate exercise bucket through the approved identity, and test that an unapproved identity cannot read or overwrite state.

State access isolation prevents unauthorized access; it is separate from the mechanism that coordinates concurrent authorized writers.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Scope the supplied readers/writers to the required ListBucket prefix and GetObject/PutObject state-object operations. Configure supplied locking permissions separately. Initialize the intended backend and provision the separate exercise bucket through the approved identity. Test that the unapproved identity cannot read or overwrite state, recording those outcomes without exposing state content. The selected bucket/key access boundary protects sensitive state; locking serves a different coordination purpose.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Locking is not the state authorization boundary. State access isolation prevents unauthorized access, while a separate mechanism coordinates authorized writers. Test unapproved read and overwrite rather than assuming backend initialization proves isolation.

video_need.reason: A short authorized/unapproved state-access comparison helps locate the storage permission boundary separately from writer locking.

teaching_notes: Keep state content private; use supplied bucket/key/prefix permissions and approved/unapproved identities.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Two authorized Terraform operations must not change shared state at the same time. Enable the S3 lock-file mechanism and test contention without bypassing another active writer.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The S3 backend supports lock-file locking when use_lockfile = true; locking is opt-in.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Set use_lockfile = true in the supplied S3 backend configuration and use the supplied s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject and s3:DeleteObject permissions on the .tflock object.

During the controlled state-changing operation that holds the lock, attempt a competing operation and verify it cannot acquire the lock or change state; do not disable locking to bypass the test.

Locking coordinates concurrent state writers; it is not an authorization boundary against identities that can directly change state objects.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Set use_lockfile = true in the supplied backend and grant the supplied GetObject, PutObject and DeleteObject permissions on the .tflock object. During the controlled state-changing operation holding the lock, start the supplied competing operation. Verify it cannot acquire the lock or change state. Do not disable locking to make the test proceed. If a lock remains from a failed operation and automatic unlocking failed, force-unlock has a specific recovery role; it is not a safe bypass for another active writer. Keep this coordination check distinct from tests of unauthorized direct state-object access.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: S3 lock-file locking is opt-in, not automatic for every backend. It coordinates concurrent writers and is not an authorization boundary. Force-unlock is reserved for a failed operation's leftover lock when automatic unlocking failed, not for bypassing an active writer.

teaching_blocks.title: A boundary that changes the interpretation
teaching_blocks.content: Force-unlock is not a safe way to bypass another active state writer; it is reserved for a lock from a failed operation when automatic unlocking failed.

video_need.reason: Two controlled authorized writers contending for the lock demonstrate serialization more clearly than a static backend setting.

teaching_notes: Use current S3 .tflock behavior; do not introduce obsolete mandatory DynamoDB locking or active-writer bypass.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A production promotion needs an authorized decision for the exact staged revision. The approval notification and the approver's authority are separate from the pipeline's wait point.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A manual approval action stops pipeline progression until an authorized approver approves; rejection or expiration fails the action.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Place an approval action between staging and production with the supplied review link or revision context and authorized approver permissions.

Verify the pipeline stops at approval and advances only after approval of the intended execution and revision.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Place the supplied manual approval between staging and production with its review link or revision context and designated approver permissions. Verify the pipeline stops at that action. After approval of the intended execution and revision, verify it advances. Rejection or expiration fails the action. Receiving a notification does not itself grant permission to approve, so check the authorized approver rather than treating every recipient as eligible.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A notification is not approval authority, and approval of one revision is not the recorded approval of another. Verify the intended execution/revision stops and advances only after its authorized approval.

teaching_blocks.title: A boundary that changes the interpretation
teaching_blocks.content: Receiving an approval notification does not itself grant permission to approve the action; approval requires the appropriate authorization.

video_need.reason: A short revision-specific approval pause and authorized decision helps verify progression while text covers the approval boundary.

teaching_notes: Use supplied approval context and permissions; do not invent expiration durations or approvers.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An incident matches an established runbook, but routine execution still depends on its preconditions and expected outcomes. Keep verification and stop decisions at each action boundary.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A runbook describes known procedures and their expected operational outcomes.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Verify the established runbook’s preconditions, execute only the approved actions and check each expected result before advancing.

On a supplied stop condition or an outcome outside the runbook’s bounds, stop routine execution and escalate with the observed evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Check the supplied runbook's preconditions before taking the first approved action. Execute only the stated approved steps and compare each actual result with its expected operational outcome before advancing. If a supplied stop condition occurs or a result falls outside the runbook's bounds, stop routine execution and escalate with the observed evidence. Record the last completed action and the result that required escalation so the next responder need not guess what happened. This example applies a known procedure safely; it does not authorize improvising further resource changes because the initial diagnosis seemed familiar.

For a passing step, record the actual result that matches the runbook before moving to the next approved action. For a failing step, preserve its output and stop/escalate according to the bounds. These branches keep the response reproducible for another operator. A runbook that initially fits the incident does not authorize continuing after its own expected-result check says the situation is outside routine execution.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A known runbook is not unconditional permission to continue. Preconditions, expected results and stop bounds govern execution. An out-of-bounds result calls for stopping and escalation with evidence, not an unapproved extension of the procedure.

video_need.reason: One established runbook execution with expected-result and stop checks benefits from a controlled incident-response demonstration.

teaching_notes: Use established runbook and owners; do not invent recovery actions or skip expected-result checks.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An isolated rehearsal restored a service, but the recovery objectives need two separate measured comparisons. Use the defined disruption start, readiness result and recovered data markers to test RTO and RPO.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Recovery verification must test both restoration time against RTO and recoverable data loss against RPO.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Using the supplied timestamps, measure elapsed time from the defined disruption start to passing service-readiness checks and compare it with RTO.

Using the supplied recovery markers, measure the gap between the disruption point and the latest recovered data point and compare it with RPO; a running service alone does not prove either objective was met.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative rehearsal, suppose disruption starts at 10:00 and the supplied readiness checks pass at 10:18. Elapsed restoration time is 18 minutes; compare that with the stated RTO, not with the data marker. If the latest recovered marker is 09:56, the gap from the 10:00 disruption point is 4 minutes; compare that with the stated RPO. With example objectives of 20 minutes RTO and 5 minutes RPO, both comparisons pass. If the marker were 09:50 instead, the service could still pass the time comparison while failing the data-loss comparison. These numbers are illustrative measurements, not AWS defaults. Retain the timestamps, marker and readiness evidence for both conclusions.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A running service alone does not prove either objective was met. Measure elapsed time to passing readiness checks for RTO and the recovered-data gap for RPO. A good result for one cannot substitute for the other.

video_need.reason: A timestamped restoration/data-marker comparison clarifies independent RTO and RPO measurements and pass/fail conclusions.

teaching_notes: Use isolated rehearsal and supplied readiness/data markers; do not substitute resource status for service checks.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A verified incident fix should lead to a factual timeline and one justified preventive action. Keep observations separate from causal conclusions so the follow-up does not overstate what the evidence established.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Post-incident analysis documents the incident’s impact, events, contributing causes and actions to reduce recurrence.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Write a timeline from supplied evidence and distinguish direct observations from causal conclusions supported by the verified fix.

Record one preventive action justified by the demonstrated cause, with an accountable owner and a way to verify completion.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Write the timeline from the supplied timestamps and observations: symptom, investigation evidence, approved correction and verified result. State which causal conclusion the verified fix supports rather than treating every nearby event as a contributing cause. Record one preventive action tied to that demonstrated cause, name its accountable owner and state how completion will be checked. If the evidence supports only one narrow cause, keep the action equally bounded. The post-incident analysis should describe impact, events, contributing causes and recurrence-reduction work, not assign unsupported blame or add unrelated improvements.

A justified preventive action should close the demonstrated recurrence path. If the verified fix supports a particular configuration error, tie the one follow-up action to preventing or detecting that error rather than selecting an unrelated improvement. The owner and verification method make the action accountable. Keep the incident timeline factual even when a causal conclusion remains narrower than the team first suspected.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A plausible causal story is not the same as a supported conclusion. Separate direct observations from conclusions backed by the verified fix, and give the justified preventive action an owner and verification method.

video_need.reason: A short observation/conclusion/action table helps tie one preventive change to verified evidence; text fully describes the analysis boundary.

teaching_notes: Use supplied evidence only; do not invent causal facts, blame or unrelated preventive work.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A restored target has passed its readiness checks, and clients now need to reach it through the approved endpoint change. Verify convergence rather than assuming every client immediately follows the new setting.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Recovery procedures include restoring service and directing clients to the recovered environment.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Confirm the restored target’s supplied readiness checks pass, perform the approved DNS or application endpoint switch and verify clients reach the restored target.

For DNS cutover, account for cached answers and TTL when testing client convergence rather than assuming every client immediately uses the new endpoint.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Confirm the restored target's supplied readiness checks before the approved DNS or application-endpoint switch. Perform that switch through the supplied procedure and test that clients reach the restored target. For a DNS switch, account for cached answers and TTL while checking client convergence. A changed DNS setting and an old client answer can coexist during caching; retain the actual client-target evidence instead of declaring all clients moved at the update request.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Endpoint configuration is not the same as verified client convergence. For DNS, cached answers and TTL matter; test clients reaching the ready restored target rather than assuming an immediate universal switch.

video_need.reason: A short ready-target cutover and client-cache timeline helps explain DNS convergence without implying an immediate universal switch.

teaching_notes: Use approved cutover procedure only after readiness; do not invent DNS record commands or TTL defaults.
